events.text: The pearl divers of the Lantern Reef go down on one breath, a stone in each hand, to the shelves where the great clams sleep. The divers' house takes one new diver a year, and this year it is choosing between you and two cousins from the next bay. The test is simple: bring up anything at all from the bottom.

choices.text: Dive to the deep shelf

ok.log: You go down until the light turns green and then blue, touch the bottom, and come up with a fist of white sand and a grin. The divers' house takes you that evening.

fail.log: Halfway down your chest burns and you kick for the light. You come up empty and coughing, and the cousins go in instead. The old divers say to come back next year.

choices.text: Ask the oldest diver how to hold a breath

effects.log: The old diver teaches you to breathe out first, all of it, and then in slowly, like filling a jar. You do not win this year. You will be able to stay under longer than anyone, later.

choices.text: Let the cousins have it and mend nets instead

effects.log: You mend the divers' nets all season and listen to their stories of the bottom. You learn where the clams are without ever getting wet.

events.text: A diver of the Lantern Reef comes up from the deep shelf with a pearl as big as a plum, faintly warm, with a light inside it that moves. The house goes silent. The old divers say that once in a hundred years the sea gives back a tear of the god who made it, and it must go to the temple. The merchants on the quay have already named a price.

choices.text: Carry it to the temple yourself

effects.log: You carry the warm pearl up the temple steps in both hands. The priests set it in the lamp above the altar, where it lights the whole island at night. Nobody on the reef forgets who brought it.

choices.text: Sell it to the merchants and share it out

effects.log: The pearl buys a new boat for every family in the divers' house, and a roof for the widow of the last diver lost. The priests grumble. The children of the reef eat well for years.

choices.text: Put it back where it was found

effects.log: You dive with it to the deep shelf and set it back in the sleeping clam. The old divers say nobody has ever done that. The reef's catch is good that year and for many after.

events.text: You are the senior diver of the Lantern Reef now, and the young ones come to you before their first deep dive with their stones in their hands and their faces grey. One of them, a boy called Tamsin, freezes on the edge of the boat and cannot go.

choices.text: Go down beside Tamsin

effects.log: You go down together, side by side, so close your shoulders touch. At the bottom Tamsin laughs, and loses half a breath, and comes up whooping. He becomes the best of them.

choices.text: Tell Tamsin there is no shame in the shallows

effects.log: Tamsin becomes a shallow-water diver and a famous finder of small perfect pearls. Years later he says your words saved his life, and you suspect he is right.

choices.text: Let the sea decide, the old way

effects.log: You say nothing and wait. After a long time Tamsin drops off the edge without a word. The old way works, mostly. You stay awake that night anyway.

events.text: The navigators of {pw_world} do not use paper. They use stick charts: frames of bent reed with shells tied where the islands are and curved sticks where the swells bend around them. The navigators' guild meets in a long house on stilts, and old Kaimo, who is blind and the best of them, says the guild needs younger hands.

choices.text: Learn the stick charts from Kaimo

effects.log: Kaimo makes you lie in the bottom of a canoe with your eyes shut and feel the swells through your back. After a month you can tell which island is over the horizon by the way the boat rocks.

choices.text: Build Kaimo a new chart frame

effects.log: You bend reed and tie shells for a week. Kaimo runs blind fingers over it and says it is wrong in four places and beautiful in all of them.

choices.text: Ask why nobody draws the charts on paper

effects.log: Kaimo laughs. 'Paper does not move,' Kaimo says. 'The sea does.' You think about that for a long time.

events.text: A swell has come out of the west that is on none of the charts, long and slow, as if something enormous had turned over far away. Boats are coming home off course. The guild argues all night about whether to rebuild every chart in the islands or wait for it to pass.

choices.text: Sail out and read the new swell

effects.log: You sail west for six days, lying in the bottom of the boat as Kaimo taught you. You come back with the shape of the new swell in your bones and tie it into the guild's master chart.

choices.text: Argue to rebuild every chart

effects.log: You win the argument, and the whole guild spends a winter rebuilding the charts of the islands. Not one boat is lost that season. The old navigators grumble and then thank you.

choices.text: Argue to wait

effects.log: You argue to wait, and in a month the strange swell fades. Two boats were lost before it did. You are right, and you are sorry, and the guild sees both.

events.text: Kaimo is dying and has asked to be laid in a canoe and pushed out on the tide, the way navigators go. Before that, Kaimo gives you the great chart of the guild, the one that hangs over the door: every island of the world in reed and shell. 'Keep it moving,' Kaimo says.

choices.text: Take the great chart and the guild

effects.log: You become master of the navigators. Every year you add a shell or move a stick. When you are old the chart is your own handwriting, and it is still right.

choices.text: Push Kaimo's canoe out yourself

effects.log: You walk Kaimo's canoe out into the surf at dawn and let the tide take it west. The whole guild stands on the beach. You hold the great chart against your chest like a child.

choices.text: Give the great chart to the youngest navigator

effects.log: You hand it to the youngest of the guild, who nearly drops it. Kaimo, hearing, laughs for the last time. 'Good,' Kaimo says. 'You learned the main thing.'

events.text: Once every seven years the islands of {pw_world} send their headmen to the Harbour Moot, held on a reef that is only dry for three days. It is where the islands settle their quarrels over fishing grounds, and this time your island has chosen you to speak, because nobody else would.

choices.text: Speak plainly for your island

effects.log: You say what your island wants and why, in fewer words than anyone. The old headmen, who are used to speeches that last a tide, are so surprised they agree to half of it.

choices.text: Listen to every island first

effects.log: You listen for two days before you speak. When you do, you know what everyone wants and what they will give up. You come home with more than you were sent for.

choices.text: Bring the reef a gift of fresh water

effects.log: You arrive with a boat full of fresh water barrels, which nobody thought to bring to a dry reef. By the third day every headman owes you a drink.

events.text: The quarrel of this Moot is the Silver Bank, the richest fishing ground in the islands, which two islands both claim by the god's own gift. Each has a priest swearing the god told them so. Tempers are rising with the tide.

choices.text: Propose they fish it in alternate years

effects.log: Alternate years. It is so simple both priests are offended. It holds for forty years, and fishermen still call it your rule.

choices.text: Propose that nobody fishes it for seven years

effects.log: Nobody likes it. But the Silver Bank, rested, is so full of fish seven years later that both islands get rich, and both claim the idea was theirs.

choices.text: Ask the priests to show the god's word

effects.log: Neither can. The Moot laughs, and the two islands, embarrassed, split the bank down the middle with a line of floats. The priests are quiet for a year.

events.text: You are an old hand at the Harbour Moot now, and this time a young headman from a far island stands up to say that the Moot is too slow, the old ways are a joke, and the islands should have a single ruler, a king of the sea.

choices.text: Argue for the Moot

effects.log: You stand and talk about every quarrel the Moot has settled without a war. The young headman sits down. Afterwards you share a fish with the young headman and both of you feel better.

choices.text: Say the young headman has a point

effects.log: You say the Moot is slow, and that slowness has kept the peace. The reef laughs. The Moot agrees to meet every five years instead of seven, which is a revolution here.

choices.text: Let the young ones decide this one

effects.log: You stay silent and let the young speak. They keep the Moot, but change it, and you go home feeling old and oddly proud.

events.text: On the island of Keel the boats are not built, they are grown: a shipwright bends living mangrove into a hull shape and waits nine years for it to thicken. The shipwright Ama Greenkeel has nine hulls growing in the shallows, and needs someone to tend them who will still be around in nine years.

choices.text: Become Ama's apprentice

effects.log: You learn to bend a branch a finger's width a month, to coax roots out of the way of a keel, and to talk to the trees, which Ama insists on. You get very patient and very wet.

choices.text: Buy a hull that is half grown

effects.log: Ama sells you a hull with five years still to grow. You visit it every week. It is the slowest purchase of your life.

choices.text: Ask why nobody just cuts timber

effects.log: Ama says a grown boat knows the sea, because it grew in it, and will never sink. You think that is a story. Then you notice nobody on Keel has ever drowned.

events.text: A storm tears through the shallows of Keel and three of the growing hulls are ripped half out of the mud. Ama is old now, and sits on the beach in the rain looking at nine years of work lying on its side.

choices.text: Replant the hulls before the roots dry

effects.log: You work two nights in the mud, packing roots back and tying the hulls upright. Two of the three live. Ama cries, which nobody on Keel has seen.

choices.text: Sit with Ama in the rain

effects.log: You sit with Ama until the rain stops. Then the two of you go out together and save the one that can be saved. It is enough.

choices.text: Cut the fallen ones into a plain boat

effects.log: You cut the ruined hulls into planks and build an ordinary boat. It leaks. Ama looks at it and says it is a fine boat for people who like bailing.

events.text: The first hull you tended is ready. The mangrove has closed around the shape of a boat, green leaves still on the gunwales, and the roots let go of the mud on the spring tide as if they knew. The whole island comes to watch it float.

choices.text: Sail it around the island

effects.log: You sail the living boat around Keel with leaves rustling at the bow. It turns before you ask it to. It knows the sea.

choices.text: Give it to the poorest fishing family

effects.log: You give the living boat away. The family sails it for sixty years, and their grandchildren plant its seeds in the shallows.

choices.text: Plant nine new hulls in its place

effects.log: You plant nine new hulls the same day. You will be old when they are ready. You find you do not mind at all.

events.text: On your island the dead go out on the evening tide in small boats heaped with flowers and a single lamp, sailing west to where the islanders say the sea ends and the god who made it is waiting. Old people build their own last boat, slowly, the way others might write a will. It is time you started yours.

choices.text: Build it yourself, plank by plank

effects.log: You build it badly and slowly and with great pleasure. Children come to watch. When it is done it is crooked and you love it.

choices.text: Ask a young shipwright to build it

effects.log: The young shipwright builds you a beautiful little boat and refuses payment. 'Everyone builds one for somebody,' the shipwright says. 'You will be my first.'

choices.text: Say you would rather be buried in the hill

effects.log: The island is scandalised. Then a few other old people admit they have always been afraid of the dark water. A small hill grave appears beside the temple, and then another.

events.text: The temple keeps a long beach where the old come to sit by their boats and watch the west. The priest who keeps it asks each of them the same question, and now asks you: what do you think is out there, where the sea ends?

choices.text: The god, waiting at the edge

effects.log: 'The god, waiting,' you say. The priest nods. You do not tell the priest that you think the god will be embarrassed to see you, after everything.

choices.text: More sea, and more islands

effects.log: 'More sea,' you say. 'More islands. Somebody always lives on the next one.' The priest laughs and writes it in the book of answers, which is very long.

choices.text: Nothing, and that is fine

effects.log: 'Nothing,' you say, 'and it is a fine nothing, quiet, like a calm evening.' The priest is not shocked. Many of the old say that. Few say it so cheerfully.

events.text: A storm has wrecked a dozen last boats on the long beach, the old people's boats, years of work. The old people stand among the broken planks, saying nothing. Some of them have no years left to build again.

choices.text: Give your own boat to the oldest of them

effects.log: You give your boat to the oldest woman on the beach, who has no time to build another. She goes out in it that spring, in your crooked boat, and her family bows to you on the quay.

choices.text: Start a yard to rebuild them all

effects.log: You get the young people of the island to rebuild the old people's boats, one each. The island has never been so busy or so kind. It becomes a custom.

choices.text: Say the sea has taken its share early

effects.log: You say it, and the old people laugh, the hard laugh of people who have buried friends. Then they start building again, faster, out of spite.

events.text: The great road of the continent runs from the eastern sea to the western mountains, a hundred days on foot, and every forty miles there is a warden's post: a tower, a well, a bell and somebody who keeps all three. The post at Thornwell has been empty since its warden married away. The road council offers it to you.

choices.text: Take the post at Thornwell

effects.log: You ring the bell at dawn and dusk, keep the well clean and the tower lit, and learn the faces of a thousand travellers. It is lonely and never dull.

choices.text: Take it, and plant an orchard beside it

effects.log: You plant apple trees around the post. In ten years Thornwell is the post every traveller hopes to sleep at, and the road council sends you seedlings for the others.

choices.text: Turn it down for the road itself

effects.log: You turn it down and walk the road instead, east to west, a hundred days. You come back brown and lean and full of other people's songs.

events.text: Snow on the great road, the worst in memory, and a caravan of forty people is caught between Thornwell and the next post. Their fires are going out. The bell of the next post has stopped ringing.

choices.text: Go out into the snow with rope and lamps

effects.log: You rope yourself to the tower and walk out into the white, ringing a handbell. One by one the lost find the sound. You bring in thirty-eight of forty.

choices.text: Ring the bell all night

effects.log: You ring the Thornwell bell all night, until your arms will not lift. The caravan walks in at dawn, following the sound. Your arms ache for a week.

choices.text: Light the tower with everything you own

effects.log: You burn your furniture in the tower lamp, and the light stands up over the snow like a pillar. They find you. You sit on the floor for a winter, happily.

events.text: The road council wants to build a new road, straight and stone-paved, that would cut out Thornwell and half the old posts and save travellers eight days. The villages along the old road are frightened.

choices.text: Speak for the old road

effects.log: You speak at the council for the villages and their wells. The new road is built anyway, but it bends to pass through six of them. The villagers name a well after you.

choices.text: Speak for the new road

effects.log: You say eight days is eight days, for the sick and the old and the hungry. The new road is built. Thornwell goes quiet and you plant more apple trees for nobody.

choices.text: Ask that the old road be kept as a pilgrim way

effects.log: The council agrees: the old road becomes the slow road, for those who walk to the god's temples. Thornwell fills with pilgrims, who are better company than merchants.

events.text: In the heart of the continent stands the Great Granary, a hill of stone bins where every town gives a tenth of its harvest against the hungry years. The keepers swear an oath on the god's name never to sell a grain while anyone starves. One of the keepers has died. The towns have put your name forward.

choices.text: Swear the keepers' oath

effects.log: You swear on the god's name, in the dust of the bins, with a handful of wheat in your fist. You do not yet know how heavy a handful of wheat can be.

choices.text: Ask to see the books first

effects.log: You read the granary books for a week before you swear. You find two keepers have been selling grain on the quiet. They are gone by spring, and you swear after.

choices.text: Refuse: you would sell the grain

effects.log: You say plainly that you could not watch a full bin while someone outside had money. The keepers look at each other and say that is the right answer, but you will not hear it.

events.text: The rains fail two years running. The granary bins go down like a tide going out. Now the great lords of the plains come with silver, offering three times the price, and the hungry villages come with nothing but their children's faces.

choices.text: Open the bins to the villages

effects.log: You open the bins to the hungry first and lock them against the lords. The lords are furious. Nobody in the plains starves that year, and the villages never forget.

choices.text: Sell a little to the lords, to buy more grain

effects.log: You sell a little to the lords at their wild price and buy grain from the far coast with the money. It works. You lie awake for a year anyway.

choices.text: Ration it to everyone alike

effects.log: Lord and farmer get the same bowl. The lords complain. The farmers think it is a miracle. It is only arithmetic.

events.text: Rain again, and good harvests, and the bins full to the roof. Young keepers are swearing the oath in the dust, as you did. They ask you what the oath is really for, since nobody has been hungry for years.

choices.text: Tell them about the dry years

effects.log: You tell them about the children's faces at the gate. The young keepers are quiet for a long time and swear the oath with both hands.

choices.text: Tell them it is for the god

effects.log: You say the god once let a people go hungry, or so the priests say, and the oath is a promise never to be so careless. The young ones are shocked, and remember.

choices.text: Show them the empty bin you never refilled

effects.log: You kept one bin empty, swept clean, to remember. You show them. Nobody refills it after you are gone, either.

events.text: Every autumn the herds of the plains are driven from the summer grass to the winter river, three hundred miles of open country, and the drive needs every pair of hands it can find. The drovers say you have not seen the continent until you have seen it over the horns of ten thousand cattle.

choices.text: Ride with the drive

effects.log: You ride drag at the back, eating dust for a month, and then point at the front, where there is nothing ahead but grass and sky. You come back speaking drover.

choices.text: Cook for the drive

effects.log: You cook for forty drovers for six weeks. By the end they would follow you anywhere, mostly toward supper.

choices.text: Watch them go from the hill

effects.log: You watch the herd pass for a whole day, a brown river of backs, and it is still passing at nightfall. You have never felt so small or so pleased about it.

events.text: Halfway across the plains the herd smells thunder and begins to run, ten thousand cattle in the dark, the ground shaking like a drum. The drovers are shouting. Somewhere ahead is the ravine.

choices.text: Ride to the front and turn them

ok.log: You ride in the dark at the head of the stampede, shouting, swinging your pole, and the herd turns along the edge of the ravine and slows and stops. The drovers sing about it for years.

fail.log: Your horse stumbles and you are thrown in the grass, bruised and lucky. The others turn the herd. You walk the rest of the way and nobody mentions it, which is kindness.

choices.text: Sing to them, as the old drovers do

effects.log: You sing the old slow drover song into the thunder. It should not work. The cattle near you slow, and then the ones near them. The herd stops at the ravine edge, steaming.

choices.text: Get the wagons out of the way

effects.log: You drive the cook wagon and the water carts out of the herd's path. Nobody is crushed. The herd does what herds do. You are the only one who thought of the wagons.

events.text: The great drive is your drive now: your herd, your drovers, your road across the plains. The kingdoms along the way want tolls, the farmers want the herd kept off their fields, and the old drovers want everything to be as it was.

choices.text: Pay the tolls and keep the peace

effects.log: You pay. Every town along the road is glad to see you, and the drive becomes a festival in every village it passes.

choices.text: Find a new road across the empty land

effects.log: You scout a new road across land nobody owns. It is longer, harder and free. In ten years half the drives use it, and it is called your road.

choices.text: Hand the drive to the young drovers

effects.log: You give the drive to the young and ride at the back, eating dust, where you started. It is the happiest season of your life.

events.text: On the continent the dead are laid in round barrows on the open plain, and on each barrow a tree is planted: the people say the dead come back as the tree's fruit, and feed whoever eats it. The barrow fields outside your town are an orchard a thousand years old. It is time to choose your tree.

choices.text: Choose an apple, for the children

effects.log: You choose an apple. You picture children stealing your fruit for a hundred years and find the thought delightful.

choices.text: Choose an oak, for the long years

effects.log: You choose an oak, which will not bear anything useful for a century. The barrow keeper says that is the choice of people who expect to be patient.

choices.text: Choose a plain field with no tree

effects.log: You ask for a plain mound of grass, and the keeper is troubled. Then the keeper says some choose to be grass, which feeds the cattle, which feeds everyone. It is allowed.

events.text: You walk in the barrow fields often now. A child is sitting on a barrow under a pear tree, eating a pear, and asks you, with its mouth full, whether it is eating somebody's grandmother.

choices.text: Say yes, and she is delicious

effects.log: The child looks at the pear, considers, and keeps eating. 'She is very nice,' it says. You laugh until you have to sit down.

choices.text: Say the dead give, and the living take

effects.log: You tell the child that is what the barrows are for: the old giving to the young, one last time. The child goes home and plants a pear seed.

choices.text: Say nobody knows, really

effects.log: You say nobody knows what becomes of the dead, really, but the pears are good. The child nods as if that were the most sensible thing a grown-up ever said.

events.text: The barrow keeper comes to see you with a sapling wrapped in sacking: the tree you chose, grown in the keeper's nursery, waiting. Custom says the old plant their own tree in the barrow fields while they still can, so it will know them.

choices.text: Plant it with your own hands

effects.log: You plant it in a cold spring rain, slowly, and water it, and talk to it. The keeper leaves you alone with it. It knows you now.

choices.text: Ask the town's children to plant it

effects.log: Twenty children plant your tree with twenty little spades and enormous seriousness. For years after, they visit it and tell it what they have been doing.

choices.text: Plant one for a friend who has no one

effects.log: You plant a second tree, for an old friend who had no family to choose one. The keeper writes both your names on the barrow stone.

events.text: Between the floating islands of {pw_world} the post, the medicine and the gossip go by glider: great kites of silk and cane that a flier straps on and rides off the edge. The Glider Guild takes new fliers each spring on Jumping Day. Most of the island comes to watch, and the healers come too.

choices.text: Jump on Jumping Day

ok.log: You run, and the edge goes, and the wind takes you under the arms like a parent lifting a child. You land on the next island in a hedge, laughing. The guild gives you your wings.

fail.log: You run, and the wind does not come, and you drop like a stone into the cloud below, until the guild's catch-net takes you. You are bruised and famous for the wrong reason.

choices.text: Learn to build the wings first

effects.log: You spend a year in the guild's workshop stretching silk and splitting cane. When you finally jump, you do it on wings you built yourself, which makes the edge much less frightening.

choices.text: Work the catch-nets below the edge

effects.log: You work the nets that hang under the jumping place and catch three falling fliers in one spring. The guild says you have saved more fliers than most fliers.

events.text: A sickness has broken out on Far Pellow, the most distant island, and the medicine is here. The wind is wrong, the clouds are building, and the senior fliers say nobody can make that crossing until it turns.

choices.text: Fly the medicine across anyway

ok.log: You fly into the building cloud with the medicine strapped to your chest, and come out the other side with ice in your hair and Far Pellow below you. The island rings every bell it has.

fail.log: The cloud throws you back. You land on your own island in a turnip field with the medicine safe and your pride in pieces. You go again at first light, and get through.

choices.text: Tie the medicine to a kite and fly it on a line

effects.log: You and six others pay out a line a mile long, and a kite carries the medicine over the gap. It is slow, clumsy and it works.

choices.text: Wait for the wind, as the seniors say

effects.log: You wait. The wind turns at dawn, and the fliers go, and they are in time, just. You learn that the sky does not care about courage.

events.text: You are the oldest flier still jumping, and your knees tell you so every morning. The Glider Guild has asked you to make your last jump on Jumping Day and then hang up your wings over the guild door, where the old ones hang.

choices.text: Make the last jump

effects.log: You run, and the edge goes, and the wind lifts you one last time. You take the long way round, over every island you ever carried the post to. Then you hang your wings over the door.

choices.text: Give your wings to a young flier

effects.log: You strap your wings onto a young flier who has none and push the young flier gently off the edge. Your wings fly again that same morning.

choices.text: Refuse to stop

effects.log: You refuse, and keep jumping, more slowly and very carefully, for years. The guild gives up and builds you a lower edge.

events.text: The high islands of {pw_world} float above the clouds and never see rain, so they buy it: rain sellers on the low islands catch storms in great silk nets and send the water up in barrels on pulley ropes. A rain seller named Wilm Drizzle is looking for a partner with strong arms and a head for weather.

choices.text: Go into the rain trade with Wilm

effects.log: You learn to read the clouds below, to cast a net into a passing storm and haul it in heavy and dripping. You sell your first barrel to a high garden and feel like a farmer of the sky.

choices.text: Build a better net

effects.log: Your net has a funnel in the middle, and catches twice what Wilm's does. Wilm is jealous for a day and then very pleased with the partnership.

choices.text: Buy rain for the high temple's garden

effects.log: You buy a barrel of rain and give it to the high temple, whose garden has not seen water in a month. The priests hold the barrel like a newborn.

events.text: A dry year. The storms are few, and the high islands are bidding against each other for every barrel. A lord of the highest island offers to buy every drop you catch this season, at any price, for a pleasure fountain.

choices.text: Refuse the lord and sell to the gardens

effects.log: You sell to the high gardens that grow food, barrel by barrel, at the old price. The lord's fountain stays dry. The lord does not forget, and neither do the gardeners.

choices.text: Sell to the lord and give the profit away

effects.log: You sell to the lord, and buy grain for the dry gardens with every coin. The fountain plays. The gardens live. You feel clever and a little dirty.

choices.text: Call the rain sellers together to share it out

effects.log: You call every rain seller on the low islands to the guild hall and they agree on a share for each island. It is the first rain law in the sky. It holds.

events.text: The old rain sellers have a saying: every barrel goes up, but one day you go up with it. When a rain seller dies, their ashes are sent up the ropes in the last barrel and scattered over the high gardens with the rain. Wilm Drizzle has died, and left you the ropes.

choices.text: Send Wilm up with the best rain of the year

effects.log: You catch a great storm, the best of the season, and send Wilm up in it. The high gardens bloom that spring like nothing anyone remembers.

choices.text: Keep the ropes running as Wilm did

effects.log: You keep the ropes and the old prices and Wilm's dreadful jokes. The rain sellers say it is as if Wilm never left, which is a compliment, mostly.

choices.text: Teach the high islands to catch their own rain

effects.log: You go up the ropes yourself and teach the high gardeners to dig dew ponds and hang mist nets. The trade gets smaller. The sky gets fairer.

events.text: The sky islands of {pw_world} drift, slowly, so every ten years the Drift Census measures where each one has gone, and the bridges, ropes and borders are moved to match. It is the most argued-over work in the sky. The census office needs a measurer who cannot be bribed.

choices.text: Become a measurer

effects.log: You learn the star-sights and the weighted lines. You measure your first island and find it has drifted a hundred paces closer to its rich neighbour. Both islands accuse you of lying.

choices.text: Become the census office's rope-walker

effects.log: You walk the bridge ropes between islands carrying the measuring lines, with clouds below your feet. You never get used to it. You never fall.

choices.text: Turn it down: nobody likes the census

effects.log: You turn it down. Ten years later the census reaches your own island and you wish you had someone honest inside.

events.text: Two islands are drifting toward each other and will meet within your lifetime, gently, like boats coming alongside. One is a kingdom of farmers. The other is a kingdom of priests. Both want the census to say the other one is doing the drifting.

choices.text: Measure honestly and publish it

effects.log: You publish the truth: both are drifting, equally. Both kingdoms are furious, which is how you know you are right.

choices.text: Propose a shared field where they meet

effects.log: You suggest that where the islands touch, the land belongs to both. It takes eleven years to agree. The shared field becomes the best market in the sky.

choices.text: Ask the priests what the god intended

effects.log: The priests say the god meant the islands to drift into each other's arms. The farmers say the god meant no such thing. The argument becomes a famous song.

events.text: The day comes: the two islands touch, with a long soft grinding like a ship against a quay. People from both sides stand on the edges, waiting to see who will step across first.

choices.text: Step across first

effects.log: You step across the seam between the islands, and the crowd laughs, and then both sides are crossing, shaking hands, staring at each other's hats.

choices.text: Hand the first step to two children

effects.log: Two children, one from each island, step across together while the grown-ups watch. It becomes the way every meeting of islands begins.

choices.text: Measure the seam one last time

effects.log: You measure the seam while everyone else celebrates. It is exactly where you said it would be. Nobody notices but you, and that is enough.

events.text: In the sky the dead are not buried, because there is no deep earth to bury them in. They are given to the wind: dressed in a shroud sewn with feathers and let go from the Edge of Farewells at dawn, into the sea of cloud. The sky folk say the wind carries them to the god's own island, which nobody has seen. The old sew their own shrouds.

choices.text: Sew your shroud with your own feathers

effects.log: You gather feathers for a year, one from every bird that comes to your window, and sew them into a shroud of every colour in the sky. It is the most beautiful thing you own.

choices.text: Ask the young to bring you a feather each

effects.log: Every child of the island brings you one feather. You sew them in with a note of who brought it. The shroud is a list of names.

choices.text: Say you would like to fall the old way, plain

effects.log: You ask for a plain shroud of white silk. The old sky folk nod: the plain ones fly furthest, they say. You hope so.

events.text: An old friend is given to the wind this morning from the Edge of Farewells. The priest sings, the shroud is lifted, and the wind takes it up instead of down, spinning, higher and higher, until it is a speck in the blue. The crowd gasps. Everyone looks at you, the oldest there, to say what it means.

choices.text: Say the god wanted that one close

effects.log: You say the god must have wanted your friend near, and everyone weeps and smiles at once. That evening the priests write it in the book of farewells.

choices.text: Say the wind was simply in a good mood

effects.log: You say the wind was in a good mood, as your friend always was. The crowd laughs through its tears. It is the right thing to say.

choices.text: Say nothing and watch until it is gone

effects.log: You watch until there is nothing to watch. The others wait with you, silent, the whole crowd, until the sky is empty. Then they go home quietly.

events.text: A young priest of the Edge comes to sit with you. The temple wants to write down what the old believe happens after the wind, before the old beliefs are lost. 'Where do they go?' the priest asks. 'Really?'

choices.text: To the god's island, beyond the clouds

effects.log: 'To the god's island,' you say, 'where nobody has to hold on to anything.' The priest writes it, and looks out over the edge for a long time.

choices.text: Down, into the clouds, and up again as rain

effects.log: 'Down into the clouds,' you say, 'and up again as rain on the high gardens. Nothing in the sky is wasted.' The priest says that is the oldest answer of all.

choices.text: Ask what the priest believes first

effects.log: The young priest goes red, and then, slowly, admits to having no idea. You both laugh. It is the most honest hour of the priest's training.

events.text: Deep under the mountains of {pw_world} run seams of sky-crystal, which glows in the dark and rings like a bell when struck. The miners of Hollowmount find it by listening: they say a good seam sings. The mine boss, a short square person named Dorrin Pick, needs a new pair of ears.

choices.text: Go down the mine with Dorrin

effects.log: You go down a thousand steps into the dark and press your ear to the rock. At first there is nothing. Then, far off, a sound like someone humming in the next room.

choices.text: Carry ore for the miners

effects.log: You carry baskets of ore up the thousand steps every day for a season. Your legs become the strongest in the valley.

choices.text: Ask why the crystal sings

effects.log: Dorrin says the crystal is the god's voice, frozen in the rock when the mountains were made, and it hums because it remembers. Dorrin says it so plainly you believe it.

events.text: You hear it: a seam singing louder than any in the mine's records, deep under the old temple. If the miners dig there, the valley will be rich for a hundred years. If they dig there, the temple may fall.

choices.text: Tell the temple and the miners together

effects.log: You bring the priests down the mine to hear it. The priests weep at the sound. They agree on one narrow tunnel, dug by hand, slowly. The temple stands. The valley grows rich.

choices.text: Keep it secret

effects.log: You keep it to yourself. Some songs, you decide, should be left to sing. You go down sometimes alone and just listen.

choices.text: Tell Dorrin and let the miners decide

effects.log: The miners vote to dig around the temple, the long way. It takes nine years. Nobody in the valley is poor after.

events.text: A rockfall in the deep levels. Six miners are trapped behind a wall of stone, somewhere, and the mine is too big to dig everywhere at once. Somebody has to listen for them.

choices.text: Press your ear to the rock and find them

ok.log: You listen for an hour, ignoring everything, until under the singing of the crystal you hear a faint tapping. 'There,' you say. They dig. All six come out alive.

fail.log: You hear only the crystal singing. They find the six two days later by luck, thirsty and alive. You never forget the hours of listening to nothing.

choices.text: Dig with your hands where the air is coldest

effects.log: You dig where the cold draught comes from, all night, until your hands bleed. You break through to the six at dawn.

choices.text: Strike the crystal so they can hear you

effects.log: You strike the seam with a hammer, and it rings through the mountain like a great bell. The trapped miners strike back. You follow the sound to them.

events.text: The high passes of {pw_world} are the only roads between the valleys, and each one is kept by a pass keeper who decides who may cross in winter and who must wait. The keeper of the Iron Saddle pass is retiring, with two bad knees and a bad temper. The valleys on both sides want someone they can trust.

choices.text: Take the keeping of the Iron Saddle

effects.log: You move into the stone hut at the top of the pass, with its great iron bell, its goats and its view of two kingdoms. You learn to tell a blizzard by the smell.

choices.text: Offer to share it with the old keeper

effects.log: You keep the pass together for three winters, and the old keeper teaches you everything, including a great many words nobody should say near goats.

choices.text: Decline: you love the valley floor

effects.log: You decline. You go up once a year to bring the new keeper bread, and stand in the wind looking at both kingdoms, and go home glad.

events.text: Winter, and a band of soldiers from the next valley arrives at the pass, wanting to cross to the other side in the snow. They say it is an errand of their king. They do not look like they are going to a wedding.

choices.text: Refuse them the pass

effects.log: You stand in the door of the hut and say no one crosses in this snow. They could push past. They do not. In spring you hear there was nearly a war, and no war, because they arrived too late.

choices.text: Let them cross and send word ahead

effects.log: You let them pass, and send a goat-boy down the other side by the short path with a warning. The other valley is ready. The soldiers come home without a fight.

choices.text: Feed them and talk them out of it

effects.log: You feed them hot soup and let them sleep. By morning they are homesick and frightened of the snow, and go home. Their captain sends you a ham every year.

events.text: The two kingdoms on either side of the Iron Saddle have made peace at last, and want to sign it at the top of the pass, in your hut, because it is the only place both can reach and neither owns.

choices.text: Host the signing

effects.log: Two kings in your hut, eating your goat cheese, arguing over the salt. The peace is signed on your table. Your table is famous afterwards.

choices.text: Ask them to add the keepers to the peace

effects.log: You ask that the pass keepers be paid by both kingdoms and obey neither. Both kings agree, to annoy each other. It becomes the law of every pass.

choices.text: Go out and milk the goats while they talk

effects.log: You leave them to it and milk the goats. When you come back the peace is signed and both kings are asleep by your fire.

events.text: Every spring the ice-cutters of {pw_world} climb to the glaciers and cut blocks of blue ice, packed in straw, to sell to the hot valleys below, where a cold drink in summer is worth a day's wage. It is hard, dangerous work, and the ice-cutters sing all the way up so the mountain knows they are coming.

choices.text: Join the ice-cutters

effects.log: You climb with them, singing badly, and cut your first block, blue as an evening. You carry it down on your back and sell it in a valley where children have never touched ice.

choices.text: Sell the ice in the valley markets

effects.log: You stay below and sell, and you are good at it: a cup of shaved ice with honey, a song, a story about the glacier. The ice-cutters say you could sell snow to a mountain.

choices.text: Ask why they sing to the mountain

effects.log: The oldest cutter says the mountain is the god's sleeping shoulder, and it is rude to cut a sleeping god's ice without saying good morning.

events.text: On the glacier this year, deep in the blue ice, there is something frozen: a shape like a lantern, or a small house, or a seed the size of a cart, glowing faintly. The cutters stop singing.

choices.text: Cut it out carefully and bring it down

effects.log: It takes ten cutters six days. In the valley the thing thaws, and opens, and is a flower the size of a door, of a kind nobody has ever seen. The temple keeps it.

choices.text: Leave it in the ice

effects.log: You say some things in the ice are the god's and not the cutters'. The cutters agree, relieved, and cut elsewhere. You visit it every spring.

choices.text: Fetch a priest up the glacier

effects.log: The priest climbs the glacier, looks into the ice for a long time, and kneels in the snow. Pilgrims come to that glacier for a hundred years after.

events.text: The glacier is shrinking. Every year the cutters climb further for their blocks, and the old say the mountain is waking up. The valleys want more ice than ever.

choices.text: Cut less, and raise the price

effects.log: You persuade the cutters to cut half as much, and the valleys pay twice. The glacier grows a little. The valleys learn to drink their water warm sometimes.

choices.text: Dig ice cellars in the valleys

effects.log: You teach the valleys to dig deep cellars and cut their own winter ice from the ponds. The glacier is left in peace. The ice-cutters are angry at you for a decade.

choices.text: Sing to the mountain, and ask it

effects.log: You climb alone and sing to the glacier all one evening. Nothing answers. But that winter the snow is the deepest in memory, and the glacier grows.

events.text: High on the cliffs above the clouds there are ledges where hermits live: one person to a ledge, a cave, a rope down to the world, and a basket on the rope for food. The villages below keep the hermits fed, and in return the hermits keep watch on the god, they say. One ledge has stood empty for years.

choices.text: Climb up and take the empty ledge

effects.log: You climb the rope with a blanket and a bowl. The first night the silence is so big you cannot sleep. By the tenth you can hear your own blood, and the wind, and something under both.

choices.text: Carry the food baskets to the ropes

effects.log: You carry baskets to the hermits' ropes every week, and one by one they start sending notes down in the empty baskets: thanks, advice, small drawings of birds.

choices.text: Climb up just for one night

effects.log: You climb up for one night and sit on the edge of the empty ledge with your legs over the clouds. You come down different, though you could not say how.

events.text: A season on the ledge. In the silence you have begun to feel something: a slow pulse in the rock, like a heartbeat, so slow that one beat takes a whole day. The other hermits, when you shout across to them, say they felt it too, long ago.

choices.text: Follow the pulse into stillness

effects.log: You sit with it until your own breath slows to match it. Something in you settles, like silt in a still pool. Your qi is clearer than it has ever been.

choices.text: Write down what you feel and send it down

effects.log: You send down pages in the food basket. The village priest copies them out. In ten years they are read in temples across the mountains.

choices.text: Decide it is only the cold

effects.log: You decide it is the cold, and wrap yourself up, and the pulse goes on anyway, patient, not minding what you call it.

events.text: A young person climbs your rope one morning, unannounced, and sits on the edge of your ledge, and asks you to teach them what the mountain says. They have climbed for two days and will not go down.

choices.text: Teach them, and give them the ledge

effects.log: You teach them for a year, and then climb down and give them the ledge. You go back to the villages with the silence still inside you, like a coin in a pocket.

choices.text: Send them down with your blessing

effects.log: You tell them the mountain says go home and be kind. They are disappointed. Years later they come back to say it was the best advice they ever had.

choices.text: Sit in silence with them until they understand

effects.log: You say nothing at all, for three days. On the fourth the young one laughs, suddenly, and climbs down. You know they heard it.

events.text: In the mountains the dead are carried up the Cairn Road to the high meadows and laid under a cairn of stones, one stone from everyone who loved them. The mountain folk say the dead keep climbing after that, peak by peak, until they reach the god at the top of the world. The old walk the Cairn Road once, while they still can, to choose their place.

choices.text: Walk the whole Cairn Road

effects.log: You walk it in eleven days, slowly, past ten thousand cairns, reading the names. At the top meadow you sit for an afternoon and choose a place with a view of everything.

choices.text: Choose a place near the bottom, by the village

effects.log: You choose a place low down, where the children come for berries. The old folk say you will have a long climb. You say you are in no hurry.

choices.text: Add a stone to every cairn of someone you knew

effects.log: You walk the road with a bag of pebbles and add one to every cairn of someone you knew. It takes you nine days and a great many pebbles.

events.text: A blizzard catches you on the high meadows near the cairns, and you shelter among them, an old person among the stones of the dead. In the night, through the snow, you are sure you see figures moving up the slope above you, climbing, with lanterns.

choices.text: Follow the lanterns a little way

effects.log: You follow, in the snow, a little way. They stop, and one of them turns, and lifts a lantern, as if to say: not yet. In the morning you walk home, very calm.

choices.text: Call out to them

effects.log: You call out the names of your dead. The wind takes the names up the mountain. One lantern, far above, swings, once. You weep, and then you sleep.

choices.text: Stay where you are and wait for dawn

effects.log: You wait among the stones, and the lanterns pass on up the mountain, and dawn comes. You tell nobody. You are not sure you could.

events.text: The village has started your cairn early, as the mountain custom is for the very old: a ring of stones in the place you chose, waiting, with a gap at its heart. People add a stone when they pass. Today a child brings one painted with your face.

choices.text: Thank the child and put it in yourself

effects.log: You set the painted stone in your own cairn with your own hands. The child is enormously proud. So, to your surprise, are you.

choices.text: Ask that your cairn be a shelter for walkers

effects.log: You ask that your stones be built into a wall that keeps the wind off walkers. The village builds it. Climbers rest there for a hundred years.

choices.text: Tell the child what is at the top of the mountain

effects.log: You tell the child what the old believe: that the dead climb, and at the top the god is waiting with soup. The child decides to be a climber.

events.text: The River Folk of {pw_world} say the god taught them to farm by drawing a line in the mud with one finger, and the water followed. Every generation they dig one great canal, and this generation's is the Long Finger: forty miles across the dry country to the villages that have only ever had wells. The canal master needs diggers and a surveyor.

choices.text: Dig with the canal gangs

effects.log: You dig for a summer with three hundred others, singing the digging songs, and come home with hands like old leather and a share in the canal's water.

choices.text: Learn to survey the levels

effects.log: You learn to read the fall of the land with a water-level and a long pole. A canal is only a line that knows which way is down, and you become the person who knows.

choices.text: Feed the diggers from your plot

effects.log: You give a basket of your crop to the canal kitchens every week. The diggers learn your name and wave from the cutting.

events.text: The Long Finger has reached a hill that is not on the survey: a low green mound with an old shrine of the god on top. Going round it adds a year of digging. Going through it means moving the shrine, which no one has dared do in five hundred years.

choices.text: Survey a way round that costs only a season

effects.log: You walk the hill for a week and find a fold in the land that saves most of the year. The canal goes round, the shrine stays, and the canal master buys you supper for life.

choices.text: Move the shrine, with the priests' blessing

effects.log: You carry the shrine stone by stone to the new bank, with the priests chanting. Set on the canal's edge, it looks as if it was always meant to be there.

choices.text: Ask the village beyond what it wants

effects.log: The village beyond the hill has waited three generations. They say: go through. Then they help carry the shrine. It is the fastest anybody ever dug.

events.text: The water reaches the dry villages. The last earth wall is broken, and the river runs into the new canal like a dog let off a lead, and the children of the dry country, who have never seen running water, run alongside it, shrieking.

choices.text: Run alongside it with them

effects.log: You run with the children for a mile, shouting, and fall in at the end, and nobody cares. The dry country turns green in two summers.

choices.text: Plant the first rice on the new bank

effects.log: You plant the first row of rice on the new bank, the old way, with a prayer. The dry villages plant theirs beside it. In autumn it is the best harvest in their history.

choices.text: Walk the whole canal, checking it

effects.log: You walk the forty miles, checking every bank. You find two weak places and mend them. It is the canal that never floods, in the stories.

events.text: The River Folk have one law above all: nobody owns the river. But a family upstream has built a great mill with a wheel as tall as a house, and the river below it runs slower, and the farms below are thirsty. The village elders ask you, because you are neither upstream nor down, to settle it.

choices.text: Go upstream and talk to the millers

effects.log: The millers are proud and frightened: they have put everything into the wheel. You listen. They agree to stop the wheel every third day, so the river can run.

choices.text: Call the whole river to the water council

effects.log: You call every village on the river to the council stone, and the millers are made to stand and explain. It is very uncomfortable. It works.

choices.text: Say it is not your quarrel

effects.log: You say it is not your quarrel. The quarrel goes on two more years and ends in a fight at the weir. You think, afterwards, it could have been your quarrel.

events.text: A drought year, and the mill wheel stands still every day now, but the millers' children are hungry too, and the farmers below want the wheel pulled down for good. Feelings are high. Somebody has thrown a stone through the millers' window.

choices.text: Have the mill grind for everyone, free

effects.log: You persuade the millers to grind the whole river's grain free in the drought, in return for keeping the wheel. The river sees the mill as its own after that.

choices.text: Help the millers build a smaller wheel

effects.log: You help them build a smaller wheel that takes less water. The millers grumble and grind half as much, and keep their house.

choices.text: Pull the wheel down with the farmers

effects.log: You help pull the wheel down. The river runs free. The millers leave the valley, and you see them sometimes, in the market, and look away.

events.text: Years later the millers' eldest comes back to the river, grown, and asks the water council for the right to build again, a new kind of mill that floats on the river and takes nothing from it.

choices.text: Speak for the new mill

effects.log: You speak for it. The floating mill turns all year without stealing a drop. The river calls it the god's own idea, which makes the millers laugh.

choices.text: Ask them to share it with the farms

effects.log: You ask that the new mill belong to the whole river. The millers agree. It is the first thing the River Folk ever owned together.

choices.text: Say nothing and let the council decide

effects.log: The council says yes, without you. You are glad, and a little sorry you did not say so.

events.text: The River Folk say a farmer is planted, not buried. When the old die they are laid in the field they worked, and a row of the year's crop is sown over them, and the first harvest from that row is eaten by the whole village in silence. The old choose their row while they are still strong enough to hoe it.

choices.text: Choose the row by the river

effects.log: You choose the row nearest the water, where the soil is darkest. You hoe it once more, slowly, and it is the best you have ever done it.

choices.text: Choose the row by the road

effects.log: You choose the row by the road, so travellers will see your crop and wonder who grew it. The village thinks it is a very vain choice and loves you for it.

choices.text: Ask to be planted under a fruit tree instead

effects.log: You ask for a plum tree, which the River Folk think is odd but not wrong. The priest says the god planted the first tree, after all.

events.text: An old friend has been planted this spring, and today the village eats the first rice from the friend's row, in silence, sitting on the dikes. It is the custom that the oldest person present speaks one sentence at the end.

choices.text: Say what the friend grew best

effects.log: You say: 'Nobody ever grew a better argument.' The village bursts out laughing in the silence, which is shocking, and exactly right.

choices.text: Say what the River Folk believe

effects.log: You say: 'Now you are in us, and we will carry you down to the sea.' It is what is always said. It never sounds old.

choices.text: Say nothing and eat the last grain

effects.log: You eat the last grain of rice and say nothing at all. The village waits, and then understands, and rises, and goes back to the fields.

events.text: You cannot hoe any more. The young have taken over your field, and they come to you each evening to ask what the river is doing, because you have watched it for longer than anyone alive.

choices.text: Teach them to read the river

effects.log: You teach them the colour of flood water, the smell of drought, the way the reeds lean before rain. They will teach it on, long after you are planted.

choices.text: Tell them to plant your row with something new

effects.log: You tell them to plant your row with a crop nobody has tried. They grow red rice, and it does well, and the River Folk call it your rice.

choices.text: Tell them the river will tell them itself

effects.log: You say: 'Sit by it. It will tell you.' They think you are being mysterious. Then one evening one of them sits by the river and understands.

events.text: The Stone-Born of {pw_world} settle their great matters at the Shield-Moot, where every grown warrior lays a shield in a ring and speaks standing on it. Tonight the Moot will decide whether to march against the hill clans who raided the high pastures. It is your first Moot as a grown warrior.

choices.text: Speak for the march

effects.log: You speak for the march, hard and short, as the Stone-Born like it. The shields thunder. The march is voted. You feel the weight of it settle on you like armour.

choices.text: Speak for talking first

effects.log: You say a Stone-Born warrior who has never talked first has never been brave. There is a silence. Then the oldest shield-holder bangs a shield, once, for you.

choices.text: Stand on your shield and say nothing

effects.log: You stand on your shield in silence. Among the Stone-Born that is a vote too: it means not yet. Three others do it after you. The march is delayed a month.

events.text: The Moot sends a party to the hill clans before any march, and you are in it. The hill clans meet you at a cold stream with their own shields, and their chief, a scarred old person, says the raid was hunger, not war.

choices.text: Offer them grazing in exchange for peace

effects.log: You offer the clans grazing on the low pasture in the hungry months. The chief stares, then laughs, and lays a shield beside yours. The raids stop.

choices.text: Challenge their chief to an honour bout

effects.log: You and the chief fight a bout with blunt staves at the stream, and the chief wins, barely, and is so pleased the clans pay for the stolen sheep.

choices.text: Report back honestly to the Moot

effects.log: You tell the Moot what you saw: thin children and empty pots. The Moot sends grain instead of warriors. Some call you soft. Nobody dies.

events.text: You are a shield-holder of the Moot now, one of the twelve who keep order in the ring. A young warrior stands up on a shield and says the Stone-Born should give up the old way of feuds altogether.

choices.text: Bang your shield for the young warrior

effects.log: You bang your shield. The ring goes very quiet. Then, slowly, the shields start: one, five, fifty. The feuds do not end that night. They begin to end.

choices.text: Argue the feuds keep the clans honest

effects.log: You argue it, well. The young warrior argues back, better. You lose, and find, walking home, that you are glad.

choices.text: Ask the young warrior to come and talk

effects.log: You ask the young warrior to your fire. You talk all night. The proposal the young one brings to the next Moot is half yours, and it passes.

events.text: The Stone-Born believe they came from the rock and go back to it. When a warrior grows old, a stone is raised for them in the Hall of Standing Stones, carved with their face while they still live, so that the stone knows who it is waiting for. The carvers have come to measure your face.

choices.text: Sit for the carvers with a stern face

effects.log: You sit as a warrior sits, jaw set. The stone that comes out is terrifying. Children dare each other to touch it.

choices.text: Sit for them laughing

effects.log: You laugh through the whole sitting, and the carvers, scandalised, carve it anyway. It is the only laughing face in the Hall. People visit it when they are sad.

choices.text: Ask them to carve the face of someone you lost

effects.log: You ask for an old shield-friend's face on the stone instead of your own. The carvers argue, then agree, and the friend stands in the Hall at last.

events.text: The Stone-Born say that on the longest night of the year the stones in the Hall talk to each other, and the old who sit among them can hear. You sit up in the Hall this longest night, wrapped in furs, among the faces of the dead.

choices.text: Listen to the stones

effects.log: Near dawn you hear it, or feel it: a slow grinding hum, like rock warming in the sun. It is not words. It is something like contentment.

choices.text: Talk to the stones yourself

effects.log: You tell the stones of the dead what has happened in the clans since they went. It takes all night. In the morning you feel as if you have finished a long letter.

choices.text: Fall asleep among them

effects.log: You fall asleep, and dream of a mountain that remembers every warrior who ever lived. You wake rested and unafraid.

events.text: Your stone stands in the Hall now, waiting. Young warriors come to touch it before their first Moot, as is the custom with the stones of the living old, and ask your blessing. One asks what the Stone-Born truly go back to.

choices.text: To the rock, which is the god's bones

effects.log: You say the rock is the bones of the god who made the world, and the Stone-Born go back to hold it up. The young warrior stands straighter.

choices.text: To the people who remember them

effects.log: You say the stone is only a reminder; the dead go back into the people who remember them. The young warrior thinks about it, and visits the Hall more often.

choices.text: Tell them to touch the laughing stone too

effects.log: You tell them to touch the laughing stone as well as the stern ones, because a warrior needs both. They do. It becomes the custom.

events.text: Among the Stone-Born a warrior may lay down the spear only once, before the whole clan, and never pick it up again. It is rare. It is honoured, and also mocked. An old shield-friend of yours, Brannoc, has decided to do it, and has asked you to stand beside them.

choices.text: Stand beside Brannoc

effects.log: You stand beside Brannoc in front of the clan while the spear is laid on the ground. There are jeers. You glare at each one until it stops.

choices.text: Try to talk Brannoc out of it

effects.log: You argue for a night. Brannoc listens to every word, and in the morning lays down the spear anyway, and thanks you for caring enough to argue.

choices.text: Lay down your own spear too

effects.log: You lay yours down beside Brannoc's. The clan is stunned. Two warriors leave in disgust. Three others, quietly, come later to ask what it is like.

events.text: The clans of the Stone-Born are at war with each other over a sacred spring, and the spearless, who will not fight, have gone to stand between the lines, unarmed. Brannoc is among them, in the cold, in the open.

choices.text: Go and stand between the lines too

effects.log: You stand in the cold between two armies of your own people, unarmed. Nobody throws. After a day, the chiefs come out to talk, because they are ashamed.

choices.text: Bring the spearless food and blankets

effects.log: You carry food and blankets out to them through the lines. Both armies let you pass. That they let you pass is the beginning of the end of it.

choices.text: Fight for your clan, as you must

effects.log: You take your place in the line. The fighting is short and bitter. Brannoc, between the lines, is not touched. You cannot meet Brannoc's eyes for a year.

events.text: Brannoc is dying, old and spearless, and the clan has come to argue about where Brannoc's stone should stand: among the warriors in the Hall, or outside it, where the spearless have always been put.

choices.text: Demand a place in the Hall

effects.log: You stand on your shield at the Moot and demand it. The vote is close. Brannoc's stone stands in the Hall, the first of the spearless, and others follow.

choices.text: Ask Brannoc what Brannoc wants

effects.log: Brannoc wants to stand at the door of the Hall, half in and half out, so everyone has to pass. The clan laughs and agrees.

choices.text: Carve Brannoc's stone yourself

effects.log: You carve it yourself, badly, with love, and set it where you think it belongs. Nobody dares move it.

events.text: The Wind Kin of {pw_world} have been writing everything down since the god first taught them letters, and the result is the Great Archive: nine towers of books nobody has ever finished counting. The archivists are starting, again, an Index of Everything, and need young eyes and steady hands.

choices.text: Join the index-makers

effects.log: You sit in a high window of the fifth tower with a pen and a stack of cards, writing down what every book is about. By winter you have done eleven hundred, and are slightly mad.

choices.text: Index only the books about the god

effects.log: You take the god's shelf, which is a whole tower on its own. You discover the Wind Kin disagree about the god in four hundred different ways.

choices.text: Say an index of everything cannot be done

effects.log: You say so. The chief archivist says it is the first sensible thing anybody has said about the Index in a century, and makes you the Index's official critic.

events.text: In the lowest cellar of the eighth tower you find a book that is in no catalogue: thin, very old, written in the first letters the god taught, and it seems to be a list of things the god meant to make, and did not.

choices.text: Read it all, slowly

effects.log: You read it in a week. A bird of glass. A sea of honey. A people who sleep in winter like bears. A kind of rain that sings. You cannot stop smiling, and you cannot say why.

choices.text: Bring it to the chief archivist

effects.log: The chief archivist holds it for a long time, then puts it in the highest tower, under lock, and lets you visit it. The Wind Kin argue about it for twenty years.

choices.text: Put it back where you found it

effects.log: You put it back. Somebody else will find it, in a hundred years, when the world is ready. You index the shelf above it as: miscellaneous.

events.text: The Index is finished, at last, after forty years: a tower of cards on its own, which is to say a tenth tower that now needs an index. The archivists are holding a feast. They want you to speak.

choices.text: Propose an Index of the Index

effects.log: You propose it. The hall laughs so hard the candles go out. Then three young archivists come up afterwards and say they would like to start.

choices.text: Read the entry for your own name

effects.log: You read your own entry aloud: a scholar of the fifth tower, who did eleven hundred cards in one winter. It is not much. It is in the Index forever.

choices.text: Thank the readers, not the writers

effects.log: You thank the people who read the books, who never get a feast. The readers in the hall stand up, embarrassed and delighted.

events.text: Among the Wind Kin no one may hold office until they have sat the Thousand Questions: three days in a cell with a brush, a lamp and a scroll of questions, from the god's first word to how to fix a leaking roof. The exam hall is opening for the year, and your name is on the list.

choices.text: Sit the Thousand Questions

ok.log: Three days, nine hundred and eighty answers, a cramp in your hand that lasts a month. Your name goes up on the wall among the passes, near the top.

fail.log: On the second day your mind goes white as the paper. You answer six hundred. Your name is not on the wall. The examiners say you may sit again in three years.

choices.text: Help the poor candidates study

effects.log: You run a study circle in a tea house for the candidates who cannot afford tutors. Four of them pass. You do not sit yourself this year.

choices.text: Write a question for the scroll instead

effects.log: You send the examiners a question: what would you ask the god, if you could ask one thing? They put it on the scroll. Every candidate after you answers it.

events.text: There is a scandal in the exam hall: a lord's heir has passed with answers bought from an examiner. The Wind Kin are furious. The council wants honest people to sit as examiners next year, and has asked you.

choices.text: Become an examiner and hunt the cheats

effects.log: You read three thousand answers by lamplight and catch nine bought ones. The lords hate you. The poor candidates stand in the street and clap when you pass.

choices.text: Propose answers be marked without names

effects.log: You propose that every answer be copied by a clerk before marking, so no examiner knows whose it is. It is adopted. It is still the rule.

choices.text: Decline: you would rather teach

effects.log: You decline and open a small school instead, for children who want to sit the exam one day. It is noisy, poor and happy.

events.text: A child from your street, the daughter of a lamp-seller, has sat the Thousand Questions and passed first of all the candidates, the youngest in a century. She comes to your door with a cake to say she read your old answers in the archive, the year she began.

choices.text: Ask which answer helped

effects.log: She says the one to the question about what you would ask the god: you wrote, why us? She says she has been trying to answer it ever since.

choices.text: Eat the cake together on the step

effects.log: You eat the cake on the step and talk about everything except the exam. It is the best afternoon of the year.

choices.text: Give her your old brush

effects.log: You give her the brush you sat the exam with. She takes it into office with her, and uses it for forty years.

events.text: The Wind Kin believe a scholar lives on in their words, which the wind of the world carries further than anything else. So every old scholar gives a Last Lecture, on any subject, in the open air on the Hill of Voices, and the young write down every word. The council has asked you to choose your subject.

choices.text: Speak on the god

effects.log: You choose the god: what the Wind Kin know, what they guess, and what they will never know. The subject is so large the council gives you a whole morning.

choices.text: Speak on something small

effects.log: You choose to speak on the common sparrow. The council is baffled. You have been watching sparrows for sixty years and you have a great deal to say.

choices.text: Ask to listen, not speak

effects.log: You ask to give your Last Lecture as questions only, and let the young answer. The council has never heard of such a thing, and agrees.

events.text: The day of your Last Lecture. A thousand people sit on the Hill of Voices, and the wind is blowing toward the city, which the Wind Kin say is a good omen: your words will carry. You stand up. Your hands are shaking.

choices.text: Speak as you planned

effects.log: You speak for three hours and do not stumble once. When you finish, the hill is silent, and then a thousand people tap their brushes on their tablets, the Wind Kin's applause, like rain.

choices.text: Throw away your notes and speak from the heart

effects.log: You throw your notes into the wind and talk to them as if they were your own children. Half of it is nonsense. The young remember every word.

choices.text: Say one sentence and sit down

effects.log: You say: 'Everything I learned, I learned by asking, so ask.' Then you sit down. There is a stunned pause, and then the questions begin, and go on until dark.

events.text: Your Last Lecture has been copied out by the young and has travelled, as the Wind Kin say words do, further than it should. A letter arrives from a town you have never heard of, from someone who heard it read aloud there.

choices.text: Read the letter aloud to your students

effects.log: The letter says: we disagreed with all of it, and argued for a month, and it was the best month of our lives. Your students cheer. You keep the letter.

choices.text: Write back, answering every point

effects.log: You write back forty pages. A correspondence begins that lasts the rest of your life, with a stranger you never meet.

choices.text: Put it in the Archive with the lecture

effects.log: You put the letter in the Great Archive beside your lecture, so that whoever reads one reads the other. It is the Wind Kin way.

events.text: The temple of the god in your town rings the dawn bell by hand, and the bell-ringer this year is {npc}, who is very bad at it: the bell goes off early, late, twice, once at midnight. The whole town knows {npc}'s name by spring. You live under the tower.

choices.text: Climb the tower and offer to help

mem.note: climbed the tower to help me ring

effects.log: You climb two hundred steps at dawn. {npc} is hanging on the rope, red-faced. Together you ring it exactly on time, for the first time all year. The town wakes up confused.

choices.text: Leave a note: the sun rises at the same time every day

mem.note: wrote me a cheeky note about the bell

effects.log: {npc} leaves a note back, under your door: not in this tower it does not. You laugh into your breakfast.

choices.text: Buy earplugs

effects.log: You buy earplugs and sleep through the year. You hear later that the bell-ringer was lovely. You will never know.

events.text: You have been ringing the dawn bell with {npc} for a season. On the feast day of the god the bell must be rung a hundred and eight times without a pause, by two ringers, and the priests have asked the two of you.

choices.text: Ring it together, counting aloud

mem.note: rang the feast bell with me

effects.log: You count aloud together, one to a hundred and eight, your hands on the same rope. At the end your arms are dead and the whole town is cheering. {npc} is looking at you, not the town.

choices.text: Ring it in a pattern of your own

mem.note: talked to me in bell

effects.log: You ring a pattern: long, short, short, long. {npc} catches it and answers. The town hears a conversation in bronze. The priests are scandalised. Everyone else loves it.

choices.text: Ask to step aside for a better ringer

effects.log: You step aside. {npc} rings with someone else, and does it well, and looks for you in the crowd afterwards, and does not find you.

events.text: The top of the tower, after the dawn bell, with the town still asleep below and the sun coming up over the hills. {npc} says the priests have offered the post of bell-keeper for life, and that it is a post for two.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to marry you, here

effects.log: You ask, at the top of the tower, with the bell still humming. {npc} says yes and rings the bell, once, which is forbidden. You are married under it in spring.

choices.text: Say you will keep the bell with {npc}, as friends

mem.note: kept the bell with me

effects.log: You keep the bell together for years as friends, which is its own kind of wonderful. The town assumes otherwise. You both let it.

choices.text: Say you are not made for towers

effects.log: You say it gently. {npc} nods and rings the bell alone that morning, slower than usual. The town notices.

events.text: When the river floods and then falls back, the River Folk hold the Flood Dance on the new mud, barefoot, to thank the god for the silt. It is messy, joyful and a famous place to fall in love. You slip in the first dance and take {npc} down with you.

choices.text: Laugh and pull {npc} up

mem.note: fell in the mud with me at the Flood Dance

effects.log: You are both covered in mud from head to foot. {npc} laughs so hard it is impossible to stand. You dance the rest of the night like that, two mud statues.

choices.text: Apologise and offer to wash the mud off at the river

mem.note: talked with me by the river all night

effects.log: You wash off at the river's edge by lantern light, and talk, and do not go back to the dance at all.

choices.text: Escape into the crowd

effects.log: You escape, mortified. Later you see {npc} dancing, still muddy, with everyone, looking as if the fall was the best thing that ever happened.

events.text: Planting season. {npc}'s family plot is next to the field you work this year, and the two of you plant facing each other across the dike, row by row, closer each day, until the rows meet in the middle.

choices.text: Plant the last row together

mem.note: planted the last row with me

effects.log: You plant the last row side by side. The old farmers on the dikes nudge each other and say the rice will be good this year.

choices.text: Leave a gift at the end of the row

mem.note: left me a clay heron

effects.log: You leave a little clay figure of a heron at the end of the row. {npc} keeps it on a shelf for fifty years.

choices.text: Plant your rows and go home

effects.log: You plant and go home. {npc} plants and goes home. The rice is good either way.

events.text: The next Flood Dance. The river is high, the mud is deep, and {npc} is waiting at the edge of it, very clean, which among the River Folk is a sign: someone means to be asked something.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to marry you, in the mud

effects.log: You ask, knee-deep. {npc} says yes and pulls you down. You are married at harvest, and every Flood Dance after, you fall in together, on purpose.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to dance, only dance

mem.note: only danced with me

effects.log: You dance all night. {npc} is a little disappointed, and very happy, and so are you. Some things wait.

choices.text: Say you are leaving the river

effects.log: You say you are going away, down the river, to the sea. {npc} says the river goes there too, and walks away into the dance.

events.text: In the Great Archive of the Wind Kin someone has been writing replies in the margins of the books you read: neat small arguments with your own notes, a day after you leave them. You finally catch them at it. It is {npc}, pen in hand, unrepentant.

choices.text: Argue back, out loud

mem.note: argued with me in the Archive

effects.log: You argue in whispers in the stacks until the archivist throws you both out. You keep arguing on the steps until dark.

choices.text: Write a reply in {npc}'s margin

mem.note: wrote to me in the margins

effects.log: You find the book {npc} is reading and write in the margin. The next day there is a reply. A correspondence in margins begins, through half the Archive.

choices.text: Report the defacing of books

effects.log: You report it. {npc} is fined and banned for a month, and gives you a long cold look on the steps. You feel righteous and slightly foolish.

events.text: The archivists have noticed the margins. Rather than punish you, the chief archivist has asked you and {npc} to write a book together, one arguing each side of the old question: did the god make the world out of love, or out of curiosity?

choices.text: Argue for love

mem.note: wrote the book with me

effects.log: You argue for love, {npc} for curiosity. You write all winter in one room. It is the most famous book of the decade, and nobody can say who won.

choices.text: Argue for curiosity
