mem.note: wrote the book with me

effects.log: You argue for curiosity, {npc} for love, which surprises you both. Somewhere in the middle of the book you change sides. So does {npc}.

choices.text: Say the question has no answer

effects.log: You refuse to write it. {npc} writes it alone, and dedicates it to the one who would not write.

events.text: The book is finished. On the last page, under both your names, {npc} has written one more line in the margin, in the neat small hand: and also, will you marry me?

choices.text: Write yes in the margin

effects.log: You write yes, in the margin, in your own hand, and the printers, who are Wind Kin, print it in every copy. You are married in the Archive among the books.

choices.text: Write: ask me again in person

mem.note: said not yet, but soon

effects.log: {npc} asks again, in person, red to the ears, on the steps. You make {npc} wait a whole breath, and then say not yet, but soon. The book is printed without the line.

choices.text: Cross it out gently

effects.log: You cross it out, gently, and write: thank you. {npc} reads it and nods, and the two of you go on arguing in margins for the rest of your lives, as friends.

events.text: There is a rope bridge between your island and the next, and on the far end there is a house with a blue door, and every evening someone comes out of the blue door to look at the sunset. One evening the someone waves. It is {npc}.

choices.text: Wave back

mem.note: waved to me across the bridge

effects.log: You wave back. The next evening, you both wave. By the end of the month you are both on the bridge, in the middle, over the clouds, talking.

choices.text: Send a paper bird across

mem.note: sent me a paper bird

effects.log: You fold a paper bird with a note in it and throw it into the evening wind. It lands on the blue doorstep. A reply comes back the same way the next night.

choices.text: Close your shutters

effects.log: You close the shutters. Some evenings you open them a crack and see {npc} on the doorstep anyway, looking at the sunset alone.

events.text: A storm tears the rope bridge between the islands, and for a month nobody can cross. Every evening {npc} stands at the far end, by the broken rope, and you stand at yours.

choices.text: Fly across on a borrowed glider

mem.note: flew across the gap to me

effects.log: You borrow a glider and jump, in the evening wind, and land on the blue doorstep in a heap. {npc} says you are a fool and holds on to you very tightly.

choices.text: Help the rope-makers mend the bridge

mem.note: mended the bridge to reach me

effects.log: You work with the rope-makers day and night. When the new bridge is strung, you are the first across, and {npc} is in the middle, waiting.

choices.text: Send lantern signals across

mem.note: talked to me with lanterns

effects.log: You signal with a lantern every night. {npc} answers. By the end of the month you have invented a whole language of lights, and the island children learn it.

events.text: In the sky islands a couple who mean to marry tie a knot in the middle of a bridge, over the clouds, and the bridge-keeper ties a ribbon on the rope to mark it. {npc} meets you in the middle of the new bridge with a length of red cord.

choices.text: Tie the knot with {npc}

effects.log: You tie the knot in the middle of the bridge, above the clouds, with both islands watching from the ends. The bridge-keeper ties the ribbon. You are married in the wind.

choices.text: Ask to tie it next spring

mem.note: gave me a promise knot

effects.log: You ask for one more season. {npc} ties a small knot in the cord and puts it in your hand. 'Then this is a promise,' {npc} says.

choices.text: Say you cannot leave your island

effects.log: You say you belong to your island, and {npc} to theirs. {npc} looks at the clouds below and says that is what bridges are for. But the cord stays untied.

events.text: Among the Stone-Born, courtship begins on the sparring ground: you ask someone to a bout with blunt staves, and if they accept, the whole clan knows what it means. {npc} has knocked you flat three times this month in the ordinary drills, and is clearly waiting.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to a bout

mem.note: asked me to a bout

effects.log: You ask. The sparring ground goes quiet. {npc} accepts, and knocks you flat a fourth time, and then helps you up, and does not let go of your hand straight away.

choices.text: Train in secret until you can win

mem.note: trained a season to beat me

effects.log: You train every dawn for a season. When you finally ask, you win the bout, and {npc} is so delighted the clan cheers.

choices.text: Pretend not to understand

effects.log: You pretend not to understand the clan's customs. {npc} gives up after a month, and you regret it after two.

events.text: A raid from the hills. You and {npc} are on the same wall, back to back, through a long cold night. When the raiders give up at dawn you are both still standing, bruised and laughing.

choices.text: Exchange shields, as shield-bonded do

mem.note: exchanged shields with me on the wall

effects.log: You exchange shields on the wall at dawn, which among the Stone-Born is nearly a vow. The clan sees it. Nobody says anything. Everyone knows.

choices.text: Carry {npc} home when {he} stumbles

mem.note: carried me home after the raid

effects.log: {npc} twists an ankle on the stair and you carry {him} home over your shoulder, both of you laughing at the indignity of it.

choices.text: Go home to sleep

mem.note: got a bowl of stew from me

effects.log: You go home and sleep for a day. When you wake, there is a bowl of stew on your step, still warm.

events.text: The Stone-Born marry at the Shield-Moot: the two stand on one shield in the ring, and if the clan bangs its shields, it is done. {npc} has brought a new shield, painted with both your clan marks, to your door.

choices.text: Stand on the shield with {npc}

effects.log: You stand on the shield together in the ring. For a breath there is silence, and then the thunder of a hundred shields. You are married in the din.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to wait until the feud is settled

mem.note: asked me to wait for peace

effects.log: You ask to wait until the clans are at peace. {npc} hangs the shield on your wall. 'It will wait here,' {npc} says.

choices.text: Say you are not ready to stand on anything

effects.log: You say it honestly. {npc} takes the shield away. The next spring the two of you still spar, as friends, and still nobody else can knock you down.

events.text: A caravan has come to town from the far side of the continent, with painted wagons and strange spices, and every night at its fire {npc} sings songs of places you have never heard of, in a voice that makes the whole square go quiet.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to teach you a song

mem.note: learned my eastern song

effects.log: {npc} teaches you a song from the eastern sea, about a fisher who falls in love with the moon. You sing it terribly. {npc} says that is the correct way.

choices.text: Sing a song of your own town back

mem.note: sang me a song of the town

effects.log: You sing an old harvest song of your town at the fire. {npc} learns it on the spot and sings it back, better. The caravan stays two extra days.

choices.text: Listen from the edge of the square

effects.log: You listen from the edge every night, and leave before the end. {npc} notices. On the last night the last song is a quiet one, sung toward the edge of the square.

events.text: The caravan is leaving at dawn for the next town, three weeks away, and {npc} has come to your door at midnight to say the caravan has room for one more.

choices.text: Go with the caravan

mem.note: joined the caravan with me

effects.log: You go. Three weeks of wagon roads and campfires and new towns, singing for your supper. You see more of the continent in a season than in your life before.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to stay a season

mem.note: asked me to stay a season

effects.log: {npc} stays a season, which a caravan singer has never done. The town has never had such a winter of songs.

choices.text: Say goodbye at the gate

effects.log: You say goodbye at the gate at dawn. {npc} sings the song you taught, walking backward down the road, until the wagons are gone.

events.text: The caravans of the continent have an old custom: a singer who means to settle sings a last song at the gate of the town they choose, and if someone answers from inside, the singer stays. {npc} is at your gate, singing.

choices.text: Answer the song and marry {npc}

effects.log: You answer the song from inside the gate. {npc} stops, and laughs, and comes in. You are married in the square with the whole caravan as guests.

choices.text: Answer the song, but as a friend

mem.note: answered me as a friend

effects.log: You answer with a friend's song, which every caravan singer knows. {npc} understands, and stays in the town anyway, and opens a music school.

choices.text: Let the song go unanswered

effects.log: You do not answer. The song ends. In the morning the caravan has gone, and on your step there is a small painted bell.

events.text: Your town is governed by the Council of Lamps: nine townsfolk who meet at night in the old temple hall, each with a lamp, and a matter is decided when enough lamps are blown out against it. One lamp has gone dark for good with the death of old Fennick the cooper, and the town has chosen you to carry it.

choices.text: Take the lamp and speak often

effects.log: You speak on every matter, the drains, the market, the bridge, the bell. The town grumbles that you never stop talking and re-elects you every year.

choices.text: Take the lamp and speak rarely

effects.log: You speak only when you have something to say. When your lamp moves, the council goes quiet. In a year it is said that your silence is worth three votes.

choices.text: Give the lamp to someone younger

effects.log: You give the lamp to a young weaver who has never held anything in public. The weaver is terrified, and then excellent.

events.text: A matter for the Council of Lamps: the priests of the god want a new temple, twice the size of the old, and want the town to pay for it. The poor quarter wants a well first. The council is split four to four, and your lamp decides.

choices.text: Vote for the well

effects.log: You keep your lamp lit for the well. The priests are cold to you for a year. The poor quarter drinks clean water, and the children stop falling sick in summer.

choices.text: Vote for the temple

effects.log: You vote for the temple. It is magnificent, and the poor quarter helps build it, for wages, and buys its own well with the wages. You did not plan that, but you take the credit.

choices.text: Propose the temple build the well

effects.log: You propose that the priests dig the well themselves as the first work of the new temple. The priests are outraged, and then rather taken with the idea. They dig it singing.

events.text: The town is growing too big for nine lamps. Some want a lord to rule it, as the great towns have. Others want more lamps, ninety, a hundred. You are the senior lamp now.

choices.text: Argue for a hundred lamps

effects.log: You argue for a hundred lamps, and win. The council hall cannot hold them, so the council meets in the square, at night, a field of lights. Travellers think it is a festival.

choices.text: Argue for a lord, chosen by the lamps

effects.log: You argue for a lord the lamps can choose and blow out again. It is a strange thing, a lord who can be blown out. It works for two hundred years.

choices.text: Blow out your own lamp and retire

effects.log: You blow out your lamp in the hall, and say the new ones should decide. They keep nine lamps, and add a tenth, for you, that is never lit and never taken away.

events.text: War has come between {pw_kingdom} and its neighbour over the White Flats, the great salt pans on the border that both crowns claim by the god's own gift. Heralds are in every square calling for soldiers. Your town must send twenty.

choices.text: Go as a soldier

effects.log: You march with the town's twenty, in borrowed boots, to the edge of the White Flats. The salt shines so white it hurts. Across it, the other army looks exactly like yours.

choices.text: Go as a carter for the army

effects.log: You drive a supply cart to the Flats. You see more of the war from behind than the soldiers do from in front, and most of what you see is waiting.

choices.text: Refuse to go, and pay the fine

effects.log: You pay the fine and stay. Some in town spit when you pass. Others, quietly, bring you bread.

events.text: The armies have faced each other across the salt for a month. Neither will cross first; the salt shows every footprint and the god, the priests say, is watching from above. Soldiers on both sides have started shouting jokes across the Flats at night.

choices.text: Walk out onto the salt under a white branch

effects.log: You walk out alone with a white branch. The salt crunches. Halfway across, a soldier from the other side walks out to meet you. You sit on the salt and share a meal.

choices.text: Shout the best joke you know

effects.log: You shout your best joke across the Flats. There is a silence, and then the other army laughs, a long rolling laugh, and someone shouts one back. Morale is never the same.

choices.text: Desert in the night

effects.log: You walk away from the war in the dark. Nobody stops you. Half the army, you learn later, had the same idea that month.

events.text: The Salt War ends, not in battle, but because both kings ran out of patience and money. The treaty is signed on the White Flats themselves. Both sides will work the salt together, and pay the god's temple a tithe of it.

choices.text: Stay and work the salt

effects.log: You stay at the Flats and become a salt worker. Your crew is half from the other kingdom. In ten years you cannot remember who was which.

choices.text: Go home and tell the town what war is like

effects.log: You tell it plainly: mostly waiting, mostly cold, mostly young people who wanted to go home. The town sends fewer to the next war.

choices.text: Keep the white branch

effects.log: You keep the white branch on your wall. Your grandchildren's children ask about it. You tell them a soldier on the other side has one too.

events.text: The old king of {pw_kingdom} has died with no clear heir, and the court is in uproar. One claimant is {npc}, a distant cousin of the old king, young, shy and honest, who has come to your town to ask the people's support and has, absurdly, been put to lodge in your house.

choices.text: Advise {npc} honestly

effects.log: You tell {npc} the truth: the people do not care who wears the crown, only whether the bread is cheap. {npc} writes it down. It becomes the first line of every speech.

choices.text: Introduce {npc} to the town

effects.log: You take {npc} to the market, the mill, the temple and the tavern. By evening the town has decided, on no evidence at all, that {npc} should wear the crown.

choices.text: Keep out of crowns

effects.log: You give {npc} supper and a bed and no advice. {npc} thanks you for being the only person in the kingdom who wanted nothing.

events.text: The great lords have chosen another claimant, and soldiers are on the road to arrest {npc}. {npc} is in your kitchen, pale, with a bag packed, asking whether to run, hide, or go to the capital and face them.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to go to the capital and face them

effects.log: {npc} rides to the capital, and stands before the lords, and says plainly what the town said about bread. The common people at the gates cheer so loud the lords give way.

choices.text: Hide {npc} in the temple

effects.log: You hide {npc} in the temple loft, with the priests' help, until the soldiers pass. The other claimant is crowned. {npc} lives quietly, and is grateful, and alive.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to run

effects.log: {npc} runs, over the border. You hear years later {npc} became a teacher in a far town, and is happy, and says your name in the morning prayers.

events.text: A royal messenger comes to your door with a sealed letter from the crown. It says that the ruler of {pw_kingdom} remembers a kitchen, and a supper, and a town, and would like you to come to the court as an adviser.

choices.text: Go to court

effects.log: You go. You are the only person at court who says what you think. It makes you enemies and makes the kingdom better. You stay ten years.

choices.text: Ask for a gift for the town instead

effects.log: You ask for a new bridge for the town, and a school. They are built in a year. Your name is on neither.

choices.text: Send back a recipe

effects.log: You send back the recipe for the supper you made {npc} that first night, and stay home. The royal cooks make it every year on the same day.

events.arc: The Envoy to the Other Crown
events.text: The council of {pw_kingdom} needs an envoy to the kingdom across the mountains, which has not spoken to yours in forty years over a quarrel nobody can quite remember. They want someone without enemies. You, it turns out, have none worth mentioning.

choices.text: Accept and study their customs

effects.log: You learn their greetings, their dishes, their gods' names for your god. When you arrive you bow the right way, and the court is so surprised it forgets to be hostile.

choices.text: Accept and bring gifts

effects.log: You bring cheese, seeds, and a choir of children. The other court is baffled and then charmed. The children sing at the queen's table.

choices.text: Decline: you would only make it worse

effects.log: You decline. The envoy they send instead makes it worse. You feel, unreasonably, responsible.

events.arc: The Envoy to the Other Crown
events.text: At the other court you find the old quarrel: forty years ago an envoy of your kingdom sneezed during the other queen's prayer to the god, and it was taken as a curse. The other court has never forgiven it. Their old queen is still alive, and still offended.

choices.text: Apologise for the sneeze, formally

effects.log: You apologise for the sneeze, at length, with a straight face, before the whole court. The old queen laughs, for the first time in forty years. The quarrel is over by supper.

choices.text: Ask the priests if a sneeze can curse

effects.log: You ask the priests of both crowns to rule on it. They debate for a month and agree the god does not mind sneezing. Peace follows, theologically.

choices.text: Sneeze, on purpose, and laugh

effects.log: You sneeze during the prayer, on purpose, and laugh. The court is horrified. The old queen stares, and then laughs too. It is a risk. It works.

events.arc: The Envoy to the Other Crown
events.text: The two kingdoms sign a treaty of friendship, and want a symbol of it: something to be set up on the mountain border, where the old roads meet.

choices.text: Propose a shared temple of the god

effects.log: A temple of the god is built on the border, with doors on both sides. The priests of both kingdoms serve in it, and argue happily for centuries.

choices.text: Propose an inn

effects.log: You propose an inn. The kings are puzzled. But the inn on the border becomes the place where the two peoples meet, marry, trade and gossip, and it does more than any temple.

choices.text: Propose a statue of the sneeze

effects.log: You propose a statue of a sneezing envoy. Both courts laugh until they cry, and build it. Children from both kingdoms climb it.

events.text: There is a quarrel in the land between those who rule and the priests of the god: the rulers want the temples to pay taxes like everyone else, and the priests say the god's house owes nothing to anyone. The quarrel has reached your town, where the tax collector and the high priest have stopped speaking.

choices.text: Side with the rulers: temples should pay

effects.log: You say it in the square. The priests are hurt. The poor, who pay plenty, are pleased.

choices.text: Side with the priests: the god's house is the god's

effects.log: You say it in the square. The tax collector is cold to you. The old devout are grateful.

choices.text: Get the two of them to talk

effects.log: You invite the tax collector and the high priest to supper, on the same night, without telling either. It is the most awkward meal of your life. It is a start.

events.text: The quarrel has grown: the temple has shut its doors in protest, and there are no weddings, no namings, no funerals in the town. People are angry at everyone.

choices.text: Propose the temple pay in work, not coin

effects.log: You propose the temple pay its tax in teaching, healing and feeding the poor. Both sides like it because it lets them say they won.

choices.text: Hold a wedding outside the shut doors

effects.log: You help a young couple marry on the temple steps, outside the shut doors, with a farmer saying the words. The priests, ashamed, open the doors the next day.

choices.text: Pay the temple's tax yourself, this year

effects.log: You pay it. The town is stunned. The quarrel ends, because nobody can keep shouting with a straight face after that.

events.text: Years later the quarrel is a story, and the arrangement you helped make is the law of the land. A young priest and a young tax clerk come to you together to ask how it really happened.

choices.text: Tell them the truth: supper and stubbornness

effects.log: You tell them about the awkward supper. They laugh. They go away and have supper together, which you suspect is the beginning of something.

choices.text: Tell them it was the god's will

effects.log: You say the god wanted it. They look at you sideways. You do not explain that you have a better idea than most what the god wanted.

choices.text: Tell them it can be undone

effects.log: You tell them every law can be undone, and should be watched. They leave serious and a little frightened, which is right.

events.text: There is no kingdom in {pw_world}: only clans and villages, each with its own headman, each going its own way. But this year the headmen of the valleys are meeting for the first time in living memory, at the god's oldest temple, because the wolves are bad and the winters are worse. Your village has sent you.

choices.text: Speak for a league of villages

effects.log: You speak for a league: shared granaries, shared watchmen, a shared feast day. Some laugh. Some do not. The ones who do not are the ones who matter.

choices.text: Speak against any king

effects.log: You say the valleys have done well without a king and should keep it so. The old headmen bang their sticks on the floor, which is agreement.

choices.text: Listen and say nothing

effects.log: You listen for three days and say nothing, and learn more about the valleys than in your whole life. On the way home you know who everybody really is.

events.text: The headmen want one of their number to be first among them, to speak for the valleys to the wolves, the weather and the strangers. Several want it badly. One of them is proposing you, because you want it least.

choices.text: Accept, for one year only

effects.log: You accept for one year. You do it well, and hand it on at the year's end, which nobody expected. It becomes the rule: one year, then home.

choices.text: Refuse, and propose a rota

effects.log: You propose that each valley takes it in turn, by lot. Nobody can argue with a lot. It is fair, and slightly ridiculous, and it lasts.

choices.text: Propose the oldest woman of the valleys

effects.log: You propose the oldest woman in the valleys, who has outlived three wolves and four husbands. Everyone is relieved. She is terrifying and wise.

events.text: The league of valleys has lasted. Now a stranger from beyond the hills has come with soldiers and a crown, offering to be king of all the valleys, for their protection. Some headmen are tempted.

choices.text: Send the stranger home with a feast

effects.log: You give the stranger the best feast the valleys can make, and a guide home. The stranger goes, puzzled, never quite understanding the refusal.

choices.text: Ask the valleys to vote

effects.log: The valleys vote, village by village, with pebbles. The crown loses by a mountain of pebbles. The stranger is impressed, and asks how it is done.

choices.text: Ask the stranger to join the league instead

effects.log: You offer the stranger's land a place in the league, as an equal. The stranger thinks about it all winter, and joins. The valleys grow.

events.text: The temples of the god in {pw_world} number {pw_temples}, and every one takes novices at the spring equinox. The novices give up their names for a year and sweep, chant and copy the god's record: that the god {pw_record}. The old priest of your town asks whether you have ever thought of it.

choices.text: Take the novice's robe

effects.log: You give up your name for a year. You sweep a thousand steps and copy the record until you know it like your own hand. It is strange to read about the god from inside.

choices.text: Help at the temple without vows

effects.log: You help the priests on feast days without taking any robe. You see the temple from the side: the gossip, the kindness, the leaking roof.

choices.text: Say the god would not want you

effects.log: The old priest laughs and says that is what everyone says, and the god has never once agreed. You think about it longer than you mean to.

events.text: Your novice year is ending. The temple offers you the full robe: a priest of the god, for life, with all that means. The night before, alone in the hall with the statue, you find you can almost remember being on the other side of the prayers.

choices.text: Take the full robe

effects.log: You take it. When you pray, now, you pray to someone you half remember, and the prayers are different from anyone else's: shorter, and more like letters.

choices.text: Take your name back and go home

effects.log: You take back your name, and keep the habits: the sweeping, the early mornings, the silence before meals. The temple says you were the best novice in years.

choices.text: Ask the statue what it wants of you

effects.log: You ask, out loud, in the empty hall. There is no answer, of course. Then you laugh, because you remember that you never knew either.

events.text: A village two valleys away has lost its priest and has nobody to bless the births or bury the dead. The temple is sending someone, and the someone is you.

choices.text: Go and serve the village

effects.log: You serve the village for years: births, weddings, burials, the leaking roof. They call you the god's own priest, which you find funnier than they know.

choices.text: Go, and teach the village to bless itself

effects.log: You teach them the words and the rites, and when they can do it themselves you go home. The village keeps a chair for you by the altar.

choices.text: Send a better priest in your place

effects.log: You find a better priest, a kind, plain one, and send them. The village is happy. You are happy for them. You wonder about it some nights.

events.text: {npc}, the high priest of the temple in your town, a person of great learning and kindness, has stopped preaching. On the steps, at dusk, {npc} tells you why: after forty years of prayer, {npc} no longer believes the god listens.

choices.text: Say the god listens, but slowly

effects.log: You say the god is slow, not deaf, and has a great many prayers to get through. {npc} laughs, despite everything, and asks how you know. You do not say.

choices.text: Say it does not matter if the god listens

effects.log: You say the prayers were never only for the god. They were for the people saying them. {npc} is quiet a long time.

choices.text: Say nothing, and sit with {npc}

effects.log: You sit with {npc} on the steps until it is dark. Some doubts are not for answering. {npc} seems grateful.

events.text: The town has noticed that its high priest no longer preaches. The other priests want {npc} removed. {npc} has asked to speak to the whole town on the next feast day, and tell them the truth.

choices.text: Stand beside {npc} on the feast day

effects.log: You stand beside {npc} as the high priest tells the town about the doubt. There is shock. Then an old weaver says to have doubted for fifty years, and is glad not to be alone in it.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to keep it quiet

effects.log: You advise silence. {npc} keeps the doubt private and goes back to preaching. The sermons are different now: gentler, and full of questions.

choices.text: Ask the priests to let {npc} stay

effects.log: You go to the other priests and argue that a doubting priest is still a priest. They agree, grudgingly. {npc} keeps the robe.

events.text: {npc} is very old now, and dying, and has asked for you, not for the priests. In the last hour {npc} says: I think I heard something, once. Last spring. I do not know what it was. Do you think it was the god?

choices.text: Say yes

effects.log: You say yes. It might even be true; you remember, faintly, listening to a great many voices. {npc} smiles and closes {his} eyes.

choices.text: Say you think the god heard every prayer

effects.log: You say every one was heard, all forty years. {npc} weeps, a little, and holds your hand, and is peaceful.

choices.text: Say it does not matter now

effects.log: You say it was enough that {npc} listened. {npc} nods. The last word is your name, said like a question that has been answered.

events.text: The great temples of {pw_world} have grown rich: gold on the statues, silk on the priests, a fee for every blessing. A small movement has begun among the poor, the Plain Folk, who pray on hillsides with no roof and no fee, saying the god never asked for gold. A Plain preacher is speaking on the hill above your town.

choices.text: Go up and listen

effects.log: The preacher is a carpenter with sawdust in their hair, and says the god made the world for free, so a blessing should be free. You find you agree with every word.

choices.text: Bring the preacher bread

effects.log: You bring bread. The preacher shares it with everyone on the hill, and somehow there is enough. You do not believe in miracles. You believe in sharing.

choices.text: Report the preacher to the temple

effects.log: You tell the priests. They thank you. You feel strange about it for a long time afterwards, and do not know why.

events.text: The Plain Folk have grown. Now the great temple has forbidden anyone to pray on the hill, and the magistrate is sending guards. The Plain Folk mean to gather anyway, at dawn, sitting on the grass.

choices.text: Sit on the hill with them

effects.log: You sit with them at dawn. The guards come, and stand, and look at a hillside of farmers praying quietly, and go home. The magistrate does not try again.

choices.text: Speak to the high priest first

effects.log: You go to the high priest and say: the god did not ask for gold, and you know it. The high priest, startled, calls off the guards. And quietly lowers the fees.

choices.text: Stay home and pray alone

effects.log: You stay home and pray in your own kitchen, without gold or roof. You find it is not different, at all.

events.text: The Plain Folk are many now, and someone has given them money to build a temple of their own. A grand one. Their preachers are arguing about whether to accept it.

choices.text: Argue to keep the hill and the sky

effects.log: You argue that the Plain Folk should keep the hill, and give the money to the poor. They do. The hill becomes the most famous temple in the land, and has no roof.

choices.text: Argue for a plain roof, nothing more

effects.log: You argue for a roof against the rain and nothing else: no gold, no fees. It is built of rough wood. It is the best-loved building in the province.

choices.text: Say they have become the thing they fought

effects.log: You say it plainly. The preachers are furious, and then ashamed, and then thoughtful. Some go back to the hillsides. Some do not.

events.text: The priesthood of the god has split over a single word in the record. One side reads the old scroll as: the god made the world and loves it. The other reads it as: the god made the world and left it. The town's temple has two altars now, at opposite ends of the hall, and the two sides pray with their backs to each other.

choices.text: Pray at the altar of the god who loves

effects.log: You pray at the near altar. The priests there are warm and a little smug. Across the hall, you feel the other side's backs like a cold wind.

choices.text: Pray at the altar of the god who left

effects.log: You pray at the far altar. The priests there are sad and very honest. They pray as if writing to someone who has moved away.

choices.text: Pray in the middle of the hall

effects.log: You kneel in the middle of the hall, between the altars, facing neither. Both sides glare. The next week three others join you.

events.text: The quarrel has turned ugly: someone has smashed a lamp on the far altar, and the two sides are shouting across the hall. The temple elders want an outsider to read the old scroll, the original, and say what it really says.

choices.text: Read the scroll for them

effects.log: You read the old scroll aloud. The word is smudged. It could be loves. It could be left. You say so. There is silence. Then someone laughs, and then everyone does.

choices.text: Say it says both

effects.log: You say the god made the world and loved it and left it, as people do with children. Both sides are offended. Both sides go home thinking.

choices.text: Mend the broken lamp

effects.log: You mend the lamp on the far altar, without a word, and light it. The near side watches. Nobody breaks anything again.

events.text: Years later, the two altars are still there, but the priests eat together now, and the children of the town play between the altars during the long prayers. The temple elders ask you to choose the words to carve over the door.

choices.text: Carve: the god made the world

effects.log: Just that. Nothing about loving or leaving. Both sides agree to it, because it is the only part they never argued about.

choices.text: Carve: ask the god yourself

effects.log: The elders are shocked, and then carve it. Pilgrims come from far away to read it, and argue on the steps.

choices.text: Carve both readings, side by side

effects.log: Both words, side by side, over the door. It is the first temple in the world to admit it does not know. It becomes the most peaceful.

events.text: A heretic is to be tried by the priests: a weaver named Imma Tallow, who has been saying in the market that the god was once a person, born and grown and dead, like anyone, before becoming a god. The priests call it the worst blasphemy. You know, better than anyone, that it is true.

choices.text: Speak for Imma at the trial

effects.log: You stand up in the temple court and say Imma may be right. The court is stunned. You are allowed to speak because nobody can think how to stop you.

choices.text: Visit Imma in the temple cell

effects.log: Imma is calm and curious and asks you why you look so strange. You say, carefully, that you think the weaver is nearer the truth than the priests. Imma laughs out loud.

choices.text: Stay quiet and watch

effects.log: You watch the trial from the back. Imma speaks well. You keep your secret like a coal in your mouth.

events.text: The priests are about to sentence Imma to exile. The high priest asks if anyone in the court has anything more to say. The hall is silent. Everyone is looking at you.

choices.text: Tell them, plainly, that you remember

ok.log: You tell them you remember being a person who became a god. The court is silent. The high priest looks at you for a long time and says the trial is ended, and walks out. Imma goes free.

fail.log: You tell them. They laugh, kindly, as at a dreamer, and exile Imma anyway, and let you go. Imma writes to you from exile: thank you for trying, dreamer.

choices.text: Argue that a god may have been anything

effects.log: You argue that the record does not say what the god was before, and the court cannot exile a weaver for filling a blank. The sentence is lightened to a fine.

choices.text: Pay Imma's fine and say nothing

effects.log: You offer to pay a fine in Imma's place, if the court will take it. It will. Imma goes home. The idea goes with the weaver.

events.text: Imma's heresy has spread, as heresies do. In the markets now people say the god was once a person, and the priests have stopped arguing. A young priest asks you, quietly: if the god was a person, could a person become a god again?

choices.text: Say yes, and that it is very lonely

effects.log: You say yes, and that it is very lonely, and that being a person is better. The young priest is quiet, and later preaches that, and it is much loved.

choices.text: Say the road is called the Maker's Stair

effects.log: You tell the young priest the old name for it. The priest goes pale, and writes it down, and goes looking.

choices.text: Say: ask the god

effects.log: You say: ask the god. The young priest looks at you oddly, for a long time, as if seeing something. Then bows, very low, and leaves.

events.arc: The Keepers of the Gift Rolls
events.text: The god blessed {pw_world} {pw_blessings} times, and the temples keep a Gift Roll of each blessing: when it came, what it was, who was there. The Keepers of the Rolls are an order of their own, careful and a little dull, and they need a new keeper with neat handwriting.

choices.text: Join the Keepers

effects.log: You copy the Gift Rolls by lamplight for a year. Every blessing, every harvest saved, every child healed. You begin to recognise the god's habits, like a friend's handwriting.

choices.text: Bring the Keepers a blessing they missed

effects.log: You bring them an old story from your town of a blessing nobody wrote down: a well that filled overnight. They add it, with your name. You are absurdly proud.

choices.text: Ask if anyone keeps a roll of the god's mistakes

effects.log: The Keepers are horrified. Then the oldest one, privately, shows you a small locked book. It is very short. It is not empty.

events.arc: The Keepers of the Gift Rolls
events.text: In the oldest roll you find a blessing written in a hand nobody knows, with a note: this one was asked for by a child, who wanted the rain to stop for one day so that a wedding could be held outside. The rain stopped.

choices.text: Find the child's descendants

effects.log: You trace the family through the rolls for a year. They are bakers in the next town, who never knew. You tell them. They hold a wedding outside, that spring, to say thank you.

choices.text: Preach about it

effects.log: You read it aloud at the feast of the gifts: the god once stopped the rain for a child's wish. The town is moved. Children start asking for small things, sensibly.

choices.text: Keep it to yourself, smiling

effects.log: You keep it to yourself. You remember it, a little. It was a good wedding.

events.arc: The Keepers of the Gift Rolls
events.text: The Keepers want to add a new kind of entry to the Gift Rolls: the blessings people give each other, since the god's have grown rare. The old Keepers think it is blasphemy. The young think it is the point.

choices.text: Vote for the new entries

effects.log: You vote yes. In a year the new roll is longer than all the god's blessings together: bread given, roofs mended, children taught. The god, you think, would be proud.

choices.text: Propose a separate roll

effects.log: You propose a separate roll, so the old Keepers are not offended. The two rolls sit side by side on the altar. Pilgrims read both.

choices.text: Write the first entry yourself

effects.log: You write the first entry: an old neighbour who shared their fire with you, one hard winter. The roll begins with a kindness to you.

events.text: The god punished {pw_world} {pw_punishments} times, and an order of priests called the Penitents believe the world must earn its forgiveness: they walk barefoot from temple to temple, fasting, carrying stones. They have come to your town, thin and solemn, and are asking for young people to join them.

choices.text: Walk a season with the Penitents

effects.log: You walk barefoot for a season, carrying a stone. You see the scars of the god's anger in every valley. Your feet harden. Your heart does something more complicated.

choices.text: Feed them and send them on

effects.log: You feed them properly, which they refuse at first, then accept, then thank you for. Penitents are hungrier than they admit.

choices.text: Ask whether the god wants their pain

effects.log: The Penitents' leader, an old woman with feet like bark, says nobody knows what the god wants. 'We carry the stone,' she says, 'so the god can see we are sorry.'

events.text: At the end of the Penitents' road there is the place of the god's worst punishment, a valley burnt to glass long ago, and the custom is to lay the stones there. Standing at the edge, you remember, faintly, the day you did it.

choices.text: Lay your stone, and ask forgiveness back

effects.log: You lay your stone, and say, quietly, to the glass valley, that you are sorry too. Nobody hears. The old woman looks at you strangely all the way home.

choices.text: Plant something in the glass

effects.log: You plant a seed in a crack in the glass. The Penitents laugh at you. In three years the crack is green. In thirty, the valley.

choices.text: Tell the Penitents the punishment was too much

effects.log: You say the god was wrong. The Penitents are shocked into silence. Then the old woman sits down on the glass and cries, for the first time in forty years.

events.text: The Penitents have changed. They still walk the roads, but now they carry seeds, not stones, and plant them in every scar of the god's anger. They ask you, an old walker of their road, what to call themselves now.

choices.text: Call them the Planters

effects.log: They take the name. Children run out to meet the Planters on the road, and carry their seed bags, and the scars of the world turn green.

choices.text: Keep the old name, to remember

effects.log: You say keep the old name: forgiveness is made of remembering. They keep it. The Penitents who plant gardens are an odd, beloved sight.

choices.text: Say they need no name

effects.log: You say a good deed needs no order. Some of them leave the order and plant on their own, everywhere, quietly. You count it a success.

events.text: The god of {pw_world} has never spoken to its people, not once, and an order of priests has given their lives to listening for the first word: the Listeners, who sit in silent halls taking turns, day and night, in case the god says something and nobody hears. They have a place for you on the dawn watch.

choices.text: Take the dawn watch

effects.log: You sit in the silent hall every dawn for a year, listening. You hear birds, rain, your own heart. You do not hear the god. You hear everything else better than ever.

choices.text: Bring the Listeners tea

effects.log: You bring the Listeners tea every morning, in silence. They come to look forward to it very much. One of them says it is the closest thing to a word from heaven they have had.

choices.text: Ask what they will do if the god speaks

effects.log: The eldest Listener thinks for a long time, and says: write it down, and then, probably, argue about it. You both laugh, silently.

events.text: One dawn, on your watch, you hear something: not a voice, but a hum, under the silence, like a great bell struck far away. It lasts as long as a breath. The other Listener on watch heard nothing.

choices.text: Write it down exactly

effects.log: You write it in the Book of Silence: a hum, at dawn, as long as a breath. It is the only entry in four hundred years. The Listeners argue about it for a decade.

choices.text: Keep it to yourself

effects.log: You keep it, like a coin. You suspect, faintly, that you know what it was: a god somewhere remembering, and almost speaking, and not.

choices.text: Tell the order you heard nothing

effects.log: You say nothing happened, because you cannot be sure, and the Listeners must not be fooled by an itch in the ear. They respect it.

events.text: The Listeners are fewer now; the young think the god will never speak. The order asks you, its oldest, whether to close the silent halls.

choices.text: Keep them open: silence is still worth hearing

effects.log: You say the halls should stay open, because a world that listens is a better world, even if no one speaks. They stay open. The young come back, slowly.

choices.text: Open them to everyone, for an hour a day

effects.log: You open the silent halls to the town for an hour a day. Farmers, children and merchants come to sit in silence. It is the most popular thing the order has ever done.

choices.text: Close them, and listen at home

effects.log: You close the halls and send the Listeners home to listen in their own kitchens. You think the god, if anything, would prefer that.

events.text: The god walked in {pw_world} {pw_appearances} times, and wherever the god set foot, the priests of the Footstep have built a small stone ring around the print. They tend the prints, sweep them, and walk the road between them, the God's Walk. A Footstep priest is looking for someone to tend a print in the hills.

choices.text: Tend the print in the hills

effects.log: You live in a hut beside a footprint in the rock, a little smaller than you expected. You sweep it every morning. Travellers come to stand in it. Children try it for size.

choices.text: Walk the God's Walk once

effects.log: You walk the whole road, print to print. At the end you realise the god walked in a circle, as if lost, or looking for something. It is a strange comfort.

choices.text: Put your own foot in a print

effects.log: You set your foot in the god's print. It fits exactly. You take it out quickly and tell nobody, and walk home very thoughtfully.

events.text: A merchant wants to buy the footprint you tend, cut it out of the rock and take it to the capital to sell views of it at a coin a time. The offer is enormous.

choices.text: Refuse: the print belongs to the hill

effects.log: You refuse. The merchant comes back with more money, and then with men, and finds the whole village sitting in a ring around the print. The merchant goes.

choices.text: Offer to carve the merchant a copy

effects.log: You carve a copy in a block of stone, very well. The merchant sells views of it in the capital and nobody can tell. You give the money to the village.

choices.text: Ask the village to vote

effects.log: The village votes to keep the print, and then, to make it fair, holds a feast for the merchant. The merchant, full of dumplings, forgets to be angry.

events.text: You are old, and the Footstep priests tell you there is a custom for the very old who have served a print: to walk once more along the God's Walk, slowly, and lay a flower in every print.

choices.text: Walk it, slowly, with a basket of flowers

effects.log: You walk it in a whole summer, a flower in every print. At the last one you sit and think: I was here before. I am glad I came back.

choices.text: Walk it with a child of the village

effects.log: You walk it with a child, who asks about every print. You make up a story for each one. The child becomes a Footstep priest and tells your stories for sixty years.

choices.text: Add your own footprint at the end

effects.log: You press your own foot into wet clay at the end of the Walk and let it dry. The priests do not know what to make of it. They keep it anyway.

events.text: In {pw_world} the god is nearly forgotten. In your town there is one temple left, very small, with one priest left in it, an old person named Hobbe who sweeps it every morning for nobody. Hobbe asks you, one day, to help lift a fallen roof beam.

choices.text: Lift the beam, and stay to help

effects.log: You lift the beam and stay for tea, and come back the next day. Hobbe teaches you the god's old prayers, which nobody else alive knows.

choices.text: Lift the beam, and ask what the temple is for

effects.log: Hobbe says it is for remembering that somebody made all this. 'Even if nobody else remembers, somebody should,' Hobbe says. You find you agree.

choices.text: Lift the beam and go

effects.log: You lift it and go. Weeks later you find yourself walking past the little temple more often than you need to.

events.text: Hobbe is dying, and has nobody to pass the temple to. Hobbe asks you, simply, if you would keep it. Sweep it. Say the prayers. Remember.

choices.text: Promise to keep it

effects.log: You promise. Hobbe dies the next week, content. You sweep the temple every morning. Children start to come and ask what it is.

choices.text: Promise to find someone who will

effects.log: You find a young widow who needs a quiet place and a purpose. The widow keeps the temple for forty years and loves it.

choices.text: Say you cannot, but write it all down

effects.log: You write down every prayer Hobbe knows, and the story of the temple. The book outlives everyone.

events.text: The little temple is not quite forgotten now. A few people come, mostly old, some young, curious. A young person asks you what the god was like, since nobody else knows.

choices.text: Tell them the truth, from memory

effects.log: You tell them, more than you should: the god was curious, careless, lonely and proud of the world. The young one listens with wide eyes and comes back every week.

choices.text: Tell them what Hobbe told you

effects.log: You tell them Hobbe's words: somebody made all this, and somebody should remember. The young one becomes the next keeper.

choices.text: Tell them to look at the world and guess

effects.log: You say: look at the world and guess. They go away, and come back with a hundred guesses, some of them right.

events.text: In {pw_world} the god is hated: statues are defaced, temples burnt, and the priests who remain keep their robes hidden under their coats. In a cellar under the bakery a handful of the faithful still pray in secret. The baker, who knows you, asks if you would like to come down.

choices.text: Go down to the cellar

effects.log: You go down. Twelve people, a candle and an old cracked statue. They pray for the god to forgive the world, and for the world to forgive the god. You find you mean it.

choices.text: Keep their secret, but do not go

effects.log: You keep the secret. When the town's guard asks about the bakery, you say it makes excellent bread, which is true.

choices.text: Ask why they still pray

effects.log: The baker says: because somebody has to tell the god the world is not all angry. You think about that all the way home.

events.text: The town's haters have heard rumours about the cellar. A crowd is gathering in the square with torches, and someone is shouting the bakery's name.

choices.text: Get the faithful out by the back way

effects.log: You lead the twelve out by the back lane and over the wall, with the cracked statue in a flour sack. Nobody is hurt. The bakery is searched and found full of bread.

choices.text: Stand in the bakery door and talk

effects.log: You stand in the door and talk to the crowd: about bread, about their mothers, about anger. Some go home. Enough go home.

choices.text: Say you know nothing

effects.log: You say nothing. The crowd finds the cellar empty: the baker had moved everyone the night before. You are relieved and ashamed.

events.text: Years pass, and the anger at the god is cooling, as anger does. The faithful of the cellar are allowed, now, to pray in the open, in a corner of the market. They ask you, one of the oldest, what to say to the people who once came with torches.

choices.text: Say: we were angry too

effects.log: You tell them to say the faithful were angry too, at the god, and prayed anyway. The old torch-carriers listen to that. Some of them come to the corner.

choices.text: Say nothing; just bake

effects.log: You tell them to bake for everyone, every feast day, and say nothing. Bread does what preaching cannot. In ten years the corner is crowded.

choices.text: Say: the god deserved some of it

effects.log: You say the god deserved some of the anger. The faithful are shocked. The old haters are disarmed. You, of all people, would know.

events.text: The people of {pw_world} love their god, and once a generation they hold the Great Thanksgiving: a whole month of feasts, songs and gifts carried to the temples. This generation's needs organisers, and the temple has asked you to run the feast in your town.

choices.text: Run it as the biggest feast ever

effects.log: You organise a feast for the whole town and three villages: a thousand tables, a hundred cooks, a song from every street. People talk about it for years.

choices.text: Run it as a feast for the poor first

effects.log: You seat the poor at the high tables and serve them first, as the god served the first people, the record says. The rich grumble and then help.

choices.text: Run it small and quiet

effects.log: You hold a quiet feast with candles and soup and silence before the meal. Some are disappointed. Some say it is the first time they felt the god was in the room.

events.text: The gifts piled at the temple for the Thanksgiving are enormous: grain, cloth, silver, carvings, children's drawings. The priests do not know what to do with them all. You suspect, quite strongly, that the god does not need any of it.

choices.text: Give the gifts away to those who need them

effects.log: You persuade the priests to give it all away, in the god's name. The town is fed and clothed for a year. The children's drawings stay on the temple walls.

choices.text: Keep the drawings, sell the rest for a school

effects.log: You keep the drawings and sell the rest. The school is built in a year, with the drawings on its walls.

choices.text: Burn a little, as the old custom says

effects.log: You burn a little of the grain on the altar, as the old custom says, so the smoke rises. You know exactly where it goes, and that it is noticed.

events.text: This is your last Great Thanksgiving, probably. You are old, and sitting at the end of a long feast table, watching the young sing to a god they have never met. A child asks you if the god knows how much we love it.

choices.text: Say the god knows, and is embarrassed

effects.log: You say the god knows, and is very embarrassed, and very pleased. The child giggles. You are telling the exact truth.

choices.text: Say the god loves us back

effects.log: You say yes, and that the god loves us back, and is sorry for the times it did not show. The child nods solemnly.

choices.text: Say: tell the god yourself, tonight

effects.log: You tell the child to say it to the stars tonight. The child does, loudly. Somewhere, you are fairly sure, it lands.

events.text: The schools of cultivation in {pw_world} grew out of the god's own teaching, the one law it left in the world: {pw_law}. Each school reads that law its own way. The School of the Open Hand in your town has lost its teacher of beginners, and the head of the school has seen you breathe.

choices.text: Teach the beginners

effects.log: You teach thirty children and two very old farmers to sit, breathe and feel the slow river of qi under the skin. It is maddening and delightful. One of the farmers is a natural.

choices.text: Ask to study before you teach

effects.log: You study a season under the head of the school, who reads the world's law in a way you have never heard. Your own cultivation deepens like a well.

choices.text: Say you learned from the world itself

effects.log: You say you learned to breathe from the world itself, and the head of the school, puzzled, asks you to show the class. The class is very confused and very interested.

events.text: A student of yours has broken through to a new stage, the first in the school for ten years, and in the moment of breakthrough said something odd: that the world's law felt like a hand on the shoulder, warm, as if the one who made it were near.

choices.text: Tell the student it may have been

effects.log: You say perhaps it was. The student weeps with joy. You do not say that your own shoulder felt warm at that moment too.

choices.text: Tell the student to write it down

effects.log: The student's account goes into the school's book, the first new entry in a century. Other schools ask to read it.

choices.text: Tell the student it was their own qi

effects.log: You say it was their own qi, settling, and nothing more. The student is a little disappointed, and becomes a very careful, very good teacher.

events.text: The head of the School of the Open Hand is stepping down, and the teachers have chosen you to lead the school. The other schools of the town, the Still Water and the Iron Root, have sent their heads to see who you are.

choices.text: Lead the school, and open it to all

effects.log: You open the school to anyone who comes: farmers, beggars, the old, the sick. The other schools are shocked. In ten years they do the same.

choices.text: Lead it, and keep the old ways

effects.log: You keep the old ways, carefully, because they were the god's. The school is steady and respected and a little dull. Nobody leaves.

choices.text: Propose the three schools teach together

effects.log: You propose a shared hall where all three schools teach their ways side by side. The heads are suspicious. The students love it.

events.text: Once a year the schools of cultivation of the province meet at the Ring of Reeds, a field by the river, to test each other: not to win, they say, but to see whose reading of the god's law is truest. It is mostly about winning. Your school wants you in the ring this year.

choices.text: Enter the ring for your school

ok.log: You win three bouts and lose the fourth to someone who moves like water. The school cheers you home anyway. You and the one who beat you share a meal by the river.

fail.log: You lose your first bout, quickly and thoroughly, to a student half your size. You lie on the reeds and laugh. Then you go and ask the student how it was done.

choices.text: Judge instead of fighting

effects.log: You sit as a judge. You see every school's way from outside, and how each is a little right. You come home wiser and with no bruises.

choices.text: Cook for the contest

effects.log: You cook for three hundred cultivators, which is like cooking for three thousand ordinary people. Every school claims you afterwards.

events.text: A quarrel at the Ring of Reeds: one school has brought a student who cultivates a forbidden way, drawing qi not from the world but from other people, a little at a time, in a handshake. The other schools want the student thrown out. The student's school says it is only a different reading of the law.

choices.text: Speak for throwing the student out

effects.log: You say a way that takes from others is not the god's way. The schools agree. The student leaves, angry. You hope the anger turns into something better.

choices.text: Offer to teach the student another way

effects.log: You offer, in front of everyone. The student is suspicious and then, slowly, curious. In a year the student draws qi from rivers, like everyone, and is good at it.

choices.text: Ask where the student learned it

effects.log: You ask. The answer is an old scroll from a ruined temple. You and the heads of the schools go and find it, and seal it, together.

events.text: The Ring of Reeds has a new custom, from your time: at the end of the contest, the winner must teach the loser one thing, and the loser must teach the winner one thing back. This year they have asked you to explain why.

choices.text: Say every reading of the law is a little right

effects.log: You say the god left one law and a hundred ways to read it, and nobody has all of them. The young cultivators nod. The old ones pretend they always knew.

choices.text: Say it is to keep the winners humble

effects.log: You say it plainly. Everyone laughs. The winner that year, a proud young person, learns to make bread from the loser, and is the better for it.

choices.text: Say nothing; just do it

effects.log: You step into the ring with the year's loser and ask to be taught something. The loser teaches you a breathing trick you have never seen. You use it for the rest of your life.

events.text: Every school of cultivation in {pw_world} claims to keep the god's own first teaching, the Founder's Scroll. Each one's scroll is different. Now a farmer ploughing an old field has turned up a clay jar, and in the jar, a scroll that looks older than any of them.

choices.text: Go to see it

effects.log: You go. The scroll is short, in the oldest letters. You can read it, though you have never learned those letters. It says: breathe, and look around you.

choices.text: Help the farmer protect it

effects.log: The schools are all on the road with offers and threats. You sit on the farmer's doorstep with a stick. Nobody gets the scroll until the farmer decides.

choices.text: Let the schools fight over it

effects.log: You stay home. The schools argue for a year. You hear about it at market and are glad you did not go.

events.text: The heads of the schools have read the jar's scroll and are horrified: it is three lines long, simple as a children's rhyme, and contradicts all their own scrolls, which are long and difficult and expensive to learn.

choices.text: Say the simple one is right

effects.log: You say the god was never complicated: it was always breathe, and look around you. Some heads are furious. The students are relieved.

choices.text: Say all the scrolls are commentary on it

effects.log: You say the long scrolls are not wrong, only long: notes in the margin of three lines. The heads of the schools take that very well.

choices.text: Say it should be given to the temple

effects.log: You say the god's words belong to everyone. The scroll goes to the temple, where anyone can read it for nothing. The schools grumble and send their students.

events.text: Children in the street now chant the jar's scroll as a skipping rhyme: breathe, and look around you, and one more line nobody can agree on. A school head asks you, privately, if you know what the third line really means.

choices.text: Say the third line is: and be kind

effects.log: You say it is: and be kind. The school head is not sure you are right. You are sure. You remember writing it.

choices.text: Say the third line is: and then go on

effects.log: You say it means: and then go on, whatever happens. The school head nods slowly and adds it to the school's teaching.

choices.text: Say the children know best

effects.log: You say to ask the children. The school head does, and gets a different answer from every one, and writes them all down.

events.text: Every faithful person in {pw_world} hopes to walk once to the First Temple, built where the world began, where the priests say the god first set foot. It is a year's journey there and back. A band of pilgrims is setting out from your town at the new moon.

choices.text: Walk with the pilgrims

effects.log: You walk with them: a widow, a pair of brothers, a cheerful thief, a priest with bad feet. By the second month they are your people.

choices.text: Go alone, by the old way

effects.log: You go alone by the old road, the slow one, sleeping in barns and temples. You see the whole of {pw_land} at walking pace. It changes you.

choices.text: Pay for a poor pilgrim to go

effects.log: You give your travel money to a poor old farmer who has dreamed of the First Temple all their life. The farmer goes. The farmer comes back glowing.

events.text: At the First Temple. It is bigger than anything you imagined, carved into a cliff, and the pilgrims around you are weeping. At its heart there is a plain flat stone, the first stone of the world, they say, where the god stood. You remember, suddenly and completely, standing on it.

choices.text: Kneel on the stone

effects.log: You kneel on the stone and the memory comes up through your knees: the dark, the first light, your own voice making things. You get up very slowly and say nothing to anyone.

choices.text: Stand on the stone, as the god did

effects.log: You stand on it. The priests gasp; nobody stands on it. You step off, and apologise, and they let it go, because something in your face frightened them.

choices.text: Watch the other pilgrims instead

effects.log: You watch the faces of the others at the stone. Every one is different. Every one is lit. You think: I made them able to look like that.

events.text: Home again, a year older. In your town, people who have walked to the First Temple wear a white thread at the wrist, and are asked, all their lives, what it was like.

choices.text: Tell them it was beautiful

effects.log: You tell them it was beautiful, which it was, and do not tell them the rest. They are content. You wear the thread till it falls off, and then tie another.

choices.text: Tell them it was the people on the road

effects.log: You say the temple was wonderful, but the people on the road were the point. It becomes a saying in the town.

choices.text: Lead the next band of pilgrims

effects.log: You lead the next band of pilgrims, and the next. You know every inn on the road and every bad-tempered ferryman. The road becomes yours.

events.text: On the pilgrim road to the great temple there is an inn for sale, cheap, because the last innkeeper died and the roof leaks and the ghost stories are excellent. The pilgrims who pass in their hundreds sleep in ditches.

choices.text: Buy the inn

effects.log: You buy it, mend the roof, and open the door. The pilgrims pour in. You learn to cook for forty, listen to forty prayers, and sleep four hours a night.

choices.text: Run it for the temple, without buying it

effects.log: You run the inn for the temple, which owns it after all, for a small wage. The priests leave you alone because you make the pilgrims happy.

choices.text: Sleep there one night and leave

effects.log: You sleep there one night. The ghost does not appear. In the morning you mend one hole in the roof, for luck, and go on.

events.text: A pilgrim has died in your inn, in the night, old and peaceful, a long way from home, with no name in the inn book but a drawing of a fish.

choices.text: Bury the pilgrim by the road, with honours

effects.log: You bury the pilgrim by the road under a stone with the fish on it. Every pilgrim who passes leaves a pebble. It becomes a small temple of its own.

choices.text: Send word along the road for the family

effects.log: You send word with every pilgrim going back. A year later a family from the coast comes, weeping, and thanks you, and stays a week.

choices.text: Ask the priests what to do

effects.log: The priests say the god takes care of pilgrims who die on the road. You do too, just in case.

events.text: The inn has become famous along the road: pilgrims say a night there is half a pilgrimage. A young pilgrim asks you why you never walked to the great temple yourself, when you have fed ten thousand who did.

choices.text: Say the temple comes to you, a pilgrim at a time

effects.log: You say the temple comes through your door every night. The young pilgrim writes it in a journal, and it ends up in a book of sayings.

choices.text: Go, at last, and leave the inn to the cook

effects.log: You go, at last, and leave the inn to the cook. At the great temple you find that half the pilgrims know your name.

choices.text: Say you already know what is there

effects.log: You say you know what is there, and smile. The young pilgrim does not understand. You do.

events.text: The great temple of the province has a relic: a comb of pale wood, which the priests say the god used to comb the clouds smooth on the first day. Pilgrims touch it for luck. You see it for the first time on a feast day, and you are absolutely certain you have never owned a comb.

choices.text: Say nothing and touch it anyway

effects.log: You touch it. Nothing happens. You decide it does not matter if the god used it. Enough people believed it to make it holy anyway.

choices.text: Ask the priest where it came from

effects.log: The priest says it was found in a cave, eight hundred years ago, by a shepherd. You say the shepherd must have had very fine hair. The priest does not laugh.

choices.text: Laugh, out loud

effects.log: You laugh out loud in front of the relic. People stare. You cannot explain, and have to leave the temple, still laughing.

events.text: The Comb of the Maker has been stolen. The province is in uproar, the priests are in tears, and there are soldiers on every road. You happen to know, because you saw them in the market, which two young fools did it.

choices.text: Find the fools and talk them into returning it

effects.log: You find them in a barn, terrified, holding the comb. You talk. They put it back on the altar at night. The priests call it a miracle.

choices.text: Tell the soldiers

effects.log: You tell the soldiers. The comb comes back. The two fools go to prison for a year, and come out very sorry, and become priests, oddly.

choices.text: Say nothing, and see what the priests do

effects.log: The priests, with no comb, start telling pilgrims that the god is in the world, not in a comb. It is their best preaching in a century.

events.text: An old shepherd's descendant comes to the temple with a confession found in a family chest: the comb was never the god's. It was the shepherd's own, left in the cave by accident. The priests are deciding whether to tell the pilgrims.

choices.text: Tell them to tell the truth

effects.log: You say the truth is holier than the comb. The priests tell the pilgrims. The pilgrims, astonishingly, keep coming, to touch the comb of the shepherd who found the god's cave.

choices.text: Tell them to keep the secret

effects.log: You say it does no harm. The priests keep the secret. You keep it too, and touch the comb on feast days, and it does no harm.

choices.text: Ask to keep the confession yourself

effects.log: You keep the confession in a box. Some day somebody will find it and argue about it for a century. That seems like the right fate for it.

events.text: In a village temple there is a clay cup that fills itself with water at dawn, every dawn, and has for five hundred years. The priests say it is the god's own cup. The village is poor, and the lord of the province wants the cup for the capital, and has offered the village a great deal of money.

choices.text: Tell the village to keep it

effects.log: You say a cup that fills itself belongs where it was put. The village keeps it. The lord is annoyed and forgets about it in a year.

choices.text: Tell the village to sell it

effects.log: You say the village needs a bridge more than a cup. They sell it. The cup stops filling in the capital. The bridge stands for three hundred years.

choices.text: Ask to see it fill

effects.log: You sit up all night and watch. At dawn, quite slowly, the cup fills from the bottom, like a spring. You know, then, that you made it, long ago, for someone who was thirsty.

events.text: A drought, the worst in a century. The wells are dry. The cup still fills at dawn, one cupful, and the village is arguing about who should have it: the sick, the children, the priests, or the lord's tax man.

choices.text: Give it to a different child each dawn

effects.log: You suggest a different child each morning. The village agrees. It is a cupful a day and it saves no one, and it is the thing that keeps the village from despair.

choices.text: Find where its water comes from

effects.log: You follow the faint damp in the temple floor to a spring deep under the hill. The village digs. The spring is enough for everyone. The cup fills on.

choices.text: Pray at the cup for rain

effects.log: You pray at the cup, with the village, for rain. It rains the third night. Nobody knows if it was the prayer. Everybody drinks.

events.text: You are old and thirsty and on your way past the village, and the priests, recognising you, offer you the dawn cupful from the cup that fills, which they have never offered anyone.

choices.text: Drink it

effects.log: You drink it. It tastes like the first water in the world. You feel, for an hour, young and strong and very far away.

choices.text: Give it to a child

effects.log: You give it to the smallest child in the temple. The priests bow to you, very low, and you never find out why.

choices.text: Pour it back into the earth

effects.log: You pour it on the temple floor. The priests gasp. Then the floor grows, in a week, a little green shoot, which becomes a tree.

events.text: A false god has come to {pw_world}, wearing the name of the real one, and its followers wear golden masks at their gatherings. Your old friend {npc} has started going. {npc} comes back glowing, saying the god is finally speaking, and asks you to come and hear.

choices.text: Go with {npc}, to see

effects.log: You go. The gathering is beautiful: light, music, a voice from the dark promising everything. You know, with every bone in your body, that it is not the god. The voice is all wrong.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what the god has asked for

effects.log: {npc} says the god has asked for faith, and silver, and the names of those who doubt. You go cold. {npc} does not notice.

choices.text: Refuse, and stay friends

effects.log: You refuse, gently. {npc} is hurt, and keeps coming to supper, and keeps asking.

events.text: {npc} has given the false god's priests everything: savings, house, and now the names of neighbours who doubt. Your name is on the list. {npc} comes to your door in tears, not sure why.

choices.text: Tell {npc} what you know

effects.log: You tell {npc}: the real god never asked for names, or silver. You know because you remember. {npc} stares at you for a long time, and then, slowly, takes off the mask.

choices.text: Take {npc} in

effects.log: You take {npc} in, and feed {him}, and say nothing about gods for a month. At the end of it, {npc} throws the mask in the river.

choices.text: Warn the neighbours on the list

effects.log: You go door to door and warn every neighbour on the list. When the masked ones come, the doors are locked. {npc} hears of it, and comes to you ashamed.

events.text: The false god's followers are fewer now, and {npc} is long out of the mask, but ashamed. {npc} wants to go to the temple of the real god and ask forgiveness, and is frightened the priests will turn {him} away.

choices.text: Walk to the temple with {npc}

effects.log: You walk with {npc} to the temple. The old priest at the door looks at {npc}'s face and opens the door wide. 'The god was fooled too, once,' the priest says. You laugh.

choices.text: Tell {npc} the god already forgives

effects.log: You say: the god forgives you. {npc} asks how you can know. You say: trust me. {npc}, for some reason, does.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to forgive {him}self first

effects.log: You say the hardest forgiveness is your own. {npc} weeps. It takes years. {npc} gets there.

events.text: The false god's temple in the city performs miracles every noon: a statue that weeps gold, a voice from the ceiling, a light that falls on the faithful who have paid the most. The crowds are enormous. A stagehand of the temple, drunk in a tavern, says too much to you about pulleys.

choices.text: Buy the stagehand another drink and listen

effects.log: You buy two more drinks and listen. Mirrors, pulleys, a priest in the roof with a speaking-trumpet, gold paint. You walk home through the city with your fists clenched.

choices.text: Go to see the miracle yourself

effects.log: You go. It is very well done. You watch an old widow give her last coins to a statue and feel sick. You know what the real god would think, because you are the real god, more or less.

choices.text: Decide it is not your business

effects.log: You decide it is not your business. Some nights, after, you think of the old widows, and the gold, and it is your business.

events.text: You know how the miracles are done. You could show the city: climb into the temple roof at noon, and pull the curtain aside, in front of the crowd. The false priests have guards, and friends in the city council.

choices.text: Pull the curtain at noon

ok.log: You climb into the roof, and at the moment of the miracle you pull the curtain away. The crowd sees the priest with the trumpet, the mirrors, the pulleys. There is a long silence, and then a roar.

fail.log: The guards catch you on the stair. You are beaten and thrown into the street, and the miracle goes on. But a dozen people saw you dragged out, and began to wonder.

choices.text: Tell the true god's priests what you know

effects.log: You tell the priests of the real god. They do not have guards, but they have pulpits. In a month the whole city is whispering about pulleys.

choices.text: Help the widows get their coins back

effects.log: You and the stagehand sneak the temple's offering box into the widows' street one night. The false priests cannot complain without saying how much they took.

events.text: The false god's temple is empty now, its gold scraped off and sold to feed the city. The council asks you what to do with the building.

choices.text: Make it a school

effects.log: The miracle temple becomes a school. The children play with the old pulleys and mirrors, and learn how they work, and are never fooled again.

choices.text: Give it back to the real god

effects.log: It becomes a temple of the real god, plain, with the curtain left open forever so everyone can see there is nothing behind it but the sky.

choices.text: Turn it into a theatre

effects.log: It becomes a theatre, which is what it always was. The actors are very good at miracles. Everyone knows they are pretend. Everyone loves it.

events.text: In {pw_world} the old have a place at the temple door: the Elders' Bench, where the oldest of the town sit in the sun and are asked for advice by anyone passing. A place has come free, as places do. The others on the bench shuffle up to make room for you.

choices.text: Sit, and give advice freely

effects.log: You sit, and give advice to everyone: young lovers, merchants, a lost goat. About half of it is good. The young say you are the best on the bench.

choices.text: Sit, and only listen

effects.log: You sit and listen. People come and tell you their troubles and go away feeling better, and you have said almost nothing.

choices.text: Say you are not old enough yet

effects.log: The bench laughs at you, which is fair. You sit down anyway, the next week, complaining.

events.text: A young person has come to the Elders' Bench with a terrible choice: to stay in the town and care for a sick parent, or to go away and become a priest of the god, which they have dreamed of since childhood.

choices.text: Tell them the god can wait

effects.log: You tell them the god has waited for everyone, and can wait for them. They stay. Years later they become a priest, and a good one, because they know about waiting.

choices.text: Tell them to go

effects.log: You tell them to go, and that the town will look after the parent. The town does, because you shame it into it. The young priest writes every week.

choices.text: Tell them you cannot choose for them

effects.log: You say you cannot choose for them. They are angry. Then, later, grateful: the choice was theirs, and they made it.
